src\cmds\README.md:5:**Command execution and output filtering.** Every module here calls an external CLI tool (`Command::new("some_tool")`), transforms its stdout/stderr to reduce token consumption, and records savings via `core/tracking`.
src\cmds\README.md:9:Does **not** own: the TOML DSL filter engine (that's `core/toml_filter`), hook interception (that's `hooks/`), or analytics dashboards (that's `analytics/`). This component **writes** to the tracking DB; analytics **reads** from it.
src\cmds\README.md:15:Rust modules exist here because they need capabilities TOML filters don't have: parsing structured output (JSON, NDJSON), state machine parsing across phases, injecting CLI flags (`--format json`), cross-command routing, or **flag-aware filtering** — detecting user-requested verbose flags (e.g., `--nocapture`) and adjusting compression accordingly (see [Design Philosophy](../../CONTRIBUTING.md#design-philosophy) and [TOML vs Rust decision table](../../CONTRIBUTING.md#toml-vs-rust-which-one)).
src\cmds\README.md:22:All command-specific filter modules that execute CLI commands and transform their output to minimize LLM token consumption. Each module follows a consistent pattern: execute the underlying command, filter its output through specialized parsers, track token savings, and propagate exit codes.
src\cmds\README.md:53: | stdout + |                                    | savings |
src\cmds\README.md:88:4. **Track** — `timer.track()` records raw vs filtered for token savings
src\cmds\README.md:116:Exit code handling is **fully automatic** when using `run_filtered()` — the wrapper extracts the exit code (including Unix signal handling via 128+signal), tracks savings, and returns `Ok(exit_code)`. Module authors just return the result.
src\cmds\README.md:257:Modules must capture stderr and include it in the raw string passed to `timer.track()`, so token savings reflect total output.
src\cmds\README.md:265:All modules accept `verbose: u8`. Use it to print debug info (command being run, savings %, filter tier). Do not accept and ignore it.

src\discover\README.md:15:When a hook sends `cargo fmt --all && cargo test 2>&1 | tail -20`:
src\discover\README.md:17:**Tokenization** — The lexer (`lexer.rs`) turns the raw string into typed tokens. It's a single-pass state machine that understands shell quoting, escapes, redirects, and operators. This is critical because naive string splitting breaks on quoted content like `git commit -m "fix && update"`.
src\discover\README.md:24:**Compound splitting** — The rewrite engine walks the tokens, splitting on `Operator` (`&&`, `||`, `;`) and `Pipe` (`|`). Each segment is rewritten independently. For pipes, only the left side is rewritten (the pipe consumer like `grep` or `head` runs raw). `find`/`fd` before a pipe is never rewritten because rtk's grouped output format breaks pipe consumers like `xargs`.
src\discover\README.md:28:1. Strip trailing redirects (`2>&1`, `>/dev/null`) — matched via lexer tokens, set aside, re-appended after rewriting

src\hooks\README.md:99:Hook processors in `hook_cmd.rs` must return `Ok(())` on every path — success, no-match, parse error, and unexpected input. Returning `Err` propagates to `main()` and exits non-zero, which blocks the agent's command from executing. This violates the non-blocking guarantee documented in `hooks/README.md`.
src\hooks\README.md:102:To add support for a new AI coding agent: (1) add the hook installation logic to `init.rs` following the existing agent patterns, (2) if the agent requires a custom hook protocol (like Gemini's `BeforeTool`), add a processor function in `hook_cmd.rs`, (3) add the agent's hook file path to `hook_check.rs` for validation, and (4) update `integrity.rs` with the expected hash for the new hook file. Test by running `rtk init` in a fresh environment and verifying the hook rewrites commands correctly in the target agent.

docs\02-usage\050_configuration.md:324:**Why this exists**: clojure-lsp discovers source paths only from the project descriptor at the workspace root (root `deps.edn` / `project.clj` / `shadow-cljs.edn` / `bb.edn`) and does not recurse for sub-module descriptors. In multi-module monorepos (e.g. `common/` + `frontend/` + `backend/` layouts), this means references in sibling modules are silently missed by `find_referencing_symbols` until a tool call happens to open one of their files. Serena works around this by walking the repo for project descriptors at startup and passing the union of their declared source paths to clojure-lsp via `initializationOptions["source-paths"]`.

README.md:34:Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.
README.md:38:Context Mode is an MCP server that solves all four sides of this problem:
README.md:40:1. **Context Saving** — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction.
README.md:41:2. **Session Continuity** — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't `--continue`, previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate.
README.md:42:3. **Think in Code** — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and `console.log()`s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 14 platforms: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator.

README.md:812:Context Mode uses [better-sqlite3](https://github.com/WiseLibs/better-sqlite3) on Node.js, which ships prebuilt native binaries for most platforms. On glibc >= 2.31 systems (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, Fedora 34+, macOS, Windows), `npm install` works without any build tools.
README.md:818:On older glibc systems (CentOS 7/8, RHEL 8, Debian 10), prebuilt binaries don't load and better-sqlite3 **automatically falls back to compiling from source** via `prebuild-install || node-gyp rebuild --release`. This requires a C++20 compiler (GCC 10+), Make, and Python with setuptools.
README.md:820:**Windows / missing binding self-heal:** if `better_sqlite3.node` ends up missing after install (e.g. `prebuild-install` not on cmd.exe PATH, no MSVC toolchain), the postinstall script and the runtime hook automatically re-fetch the prebuild and repair the binding — no manual `npm rebuild` needed (#408).
README.md:825:dnf install -y gcc-toolset-10-gcc gcc-toolset-10-gcc-c++ make python3 python3-setuptools
README.md:826:scl enable gcc-toolset-10 'npm install -g context-mode'
README.md:833:yum install -y devtoolset-10-gcc devtoolset-10-gcc-c++ make python3
README.md:834:pip3 install setuptools
README.md:835:scl enable devtoolset-10 'npm install -g context-mode'
README.md:840:Alpine prebuilt binaries (musl) are available in better-sqlite3 v12.8.0+. With the `^12.6.2` dependency range, `npm install` resolves to the latest 12.x and works without build tools on Alpine. If you pin an older version:
README.md:843:apk add build-base python3 py3-setuptools
README.md:853:| `ctx_batch_execute` | Run multiple commands + search multiple queries in ONE call. Opt-in `concurrency: 1-8` for I/O-bound batches. | 986 KB → 62 KB |
README.md:854:| `ctx_execute` | Run code in 11 languages. Only stdout enters context. | 56 KB → 299 B |
README.md:855:| `ctx_execute_file` | Process files in sandbox. Raw content never leaves. | 45 KB → 155 B |
README.md:856:| `ctx_index` | Chunk markdown into FTS5 with BM25 ranking. | 60 KB → 40 B |
README.md:857:| `ctx_search` | Query indexed content with multiple queries in one call. | On-demand retrieval |
README.md:858:| `ctx_fetch_and_index` | Fetch URL, chunk and index. 24h TTL cache — repeat calls skip network. `force: true` to bypass. Pass `requests: [{url, source}, ...]` + `concurrency: 1-8` for parallel multi-URL. | 60 KB → 40 B |
README.md:859:| `ctx_stats` | Show context savings, call counts, and session statistics. | — |
README.md:860:| `ctx_doctor` | Diagnose installation: runtimes, hooks, FTS5, versions. | — |
README.md:861:| `ctx_upgrade` | Upgrade to latest version from GitHub, rebuild, reconfigure hooks. | — |
README.md:862:| `ctx_purge` | Permanently deletes all indexed content from the knowledge base. | — |
README.md:866:Each `ctx_execute` call spawns an isolated subprocess with its own process boundary. Scripts can't access each other's memory or state. The subprocess runs your code, captures stdout, and only that stdout enters the conversation context. The raw data — log files, API responses, snapshots — never leaves the sandbox.
README.md:872:When output exceeds 5 KB and an `intent` is provided, Context Mode switches to intent-driven filtering: it indexes the full output into the knowledge base, searches for sections matching your intent, and returns only the relevant matches with a vocabulary of searchable terms for follow-up queries.
README.md:876:The `ctx_index` tool chunks markdown content by headings while keeping code blocks intact, then stores them in a **SQLite FTS5** (Full-Text Search 5) virtual table. The SQLite backend is selected automatically at runtime: `bun:sqlite` on Bun, `node:sqlite` on Linux + Node.js >= 22.13, and `better-sqlite3` everywhere else. Search uses **BM25 ranking** — a probabilistic relevance algorithm that scores documents based on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. **Porter stemming** is applied at index time so "running", "runs", and "ran" match the same stem. Titles and headings are weighted **5x** in BM25 scoring for precise navigational queries.
README.md:878:When you call `ctx_search`, it returns relevant content snippets focused around matching query terms — not full documents, not approximations, the actual indexed content with smart extraction around what you're looking for. `ctx_fetch_and_index` extends this to URLs: fetch, convert HTML to markdown, chunk, index. The raw page never enters context. Use the `contentType` parameter to filter results by type (e.g. `code` or `prose`).
README.md:884:- **Porter stemming** — FTS5 MATCH with porter tokenizer. "caching" matches "cached", "caches", "cach".
README.md:895:Levenshtein distance corrects typos before re-searching. "kuberntes" becomes "kubernetes", "autentication" becomes "authentication".
README.md:903:Indexed content persists in a per-project SQLite database at `~/.context-mode/content/`. When `ctx_fetch_and_index` is called for a URL that was already indexed within the last 24 hours, the fetch is skipped entirely. The model searches the existing index directly.
README.md:905:- **Fresh (<24h):** Returns a cache hint (0.3KB) instead of re-fetching (48KB+). Model proceeds to `ctx_search`.
README.md:907:- **`force: true`:** Bypasses cache and re-fetches regardless of TTL.
README.md:910:This means `--continue` sessions preserve indexed docs across restarts. No re-fetching, no wasted context tokens.
README.md:912:`ctx_stats` reports cache performance separately: hits, data avoided, network requests saved, and total context savings including cache.
README.md:918:- **Calls 9+:** Blocked — redirects to `ctx_batch_execute`
README.md:926:> Resuming a non-latest session via `/resume <picker>` works the same way: the SessionStart hook detects the empty live-event table for the freshly issued session id and falls back to the most recent unconsumed snapshot for the project (`session_resume` table). The picker selects the conversation; context-mode rehydrates the prior working state.
README.md:928:Session continuity requires 5 hooks working together:
README.md:932:| **PreToolUse** | Enforces sandbox routing before tool execution | Yes | -- | -- | -- | Yes | -- | -- | -- | Yes | -- | Yes | -- | ✓ (via tool_call event) |
README.md:933:| **PostToolUse** | Captures events after each tool call | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Plugin | Plugin | Plugin | Yes | -- | Yes | -- | ✓ (via tool_result event) |
README.md:935:| **PreCompact** | Builds snapshot before compaction | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | -- | Plugin | Plugin | Plugin | -- | -- | -- | -- | ✓ (via session_before_compact) |
README.md:936:| **SessionStart** | Restores state after compaction or resume | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | -- | ✓ (via experimental.chat.system.transform) | ✓ (via experimental.chat.system.transform) | Plugin | Yes | -- | -- | -- | ✓ (via session_start event) |
README.md:939:> **Note:** Full session continuity (capture + snapshot + restore) works on **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**, **VS Code Copilot**, **JetBrains Copilot**, **OpenCode**, and **KiloCode**. **OpenCode** and **KiloCode** use `experimental.chat.system.transform` as a SessionStart surrogate to inject the routing block and restore prior sessions, plus `chat.message` for user-prompt capture; full SessionStart hook support is not yet available ([#14808](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/14808), [#5409](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/5409)), but prior-session continuity and user-decision capture work fully. **Cursor** captures tool events via `preToolUse`/`postToolUse`, but `sessionStart` is currently rejected by Cursor's validator ([forum report](https://forum.cursor.com/t/unknown-hook-type-sessionstart/149566)), so session restore after compaction is not available yet. **OpenClaw** uses native gateway plugin hooks (`api.on()`) for full session continuity. **Pi Coding Agent** provides high session continuity via extension hooks (`tool_call`, `tool_result`, `session_start`, `session_before_compact`). **Codex CLI** provides partial hook-based session tracking through PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, and Stop; MCP tools work. **Antigravity**, **Kiro**, and **Zed** have no hook support in the current release, so session tracking is not available.
README.md:944:Every tool call passes through hooks that extract structured events:
README.md:948:| **Files** | read, edit, write, glob, grep | Critical (P1) | PostToolUse |
README.md:949:| **Tasks** | create, update, complete | Critical (P1) | PostToolUse |
README.md:950:| **Plans** | enter, exit, approved, rejected, file write | Critical (P1) | PostToolUse |
README.md:951:| **Rules** | CLAUDE.md / GEMINI.md / AGENTS.md paths + content | Critical (P1) | SessionStart |
README.md:954:| **Git** | checkout, commit, merge, rebase, stash, push, pull, diff, status | High (P2) | PostToolUse |
README.md:955:| **Errors** | Tool failures, non-zero exit codes | High (P2) | PostToolUse |
README.md:956:| **Error Resolution** | Error → fix pairs detected across sequential tool calls | High (P2) | PostToolUse |
README.md:957:| **Constraints** | Discovered limitations ("not supported", "permission denied") | High (P2) | PostToolUse |
README.md:959:| **Rejected Approaches** | Tool calls denied by user (PreToolUse → PostToolUse marker) | High (P2) | PreToolUse |

README.md:1022:**Claude Code** — Full session support. All 5 hook types fire, capturing tool events, user decisions, building compaction snapshots, and restoring state after compaction, `--continue`, `--resume`, or `/resume`.
README.md:1024:**Gemini CLI** — High coverage. PostToolUse (AfterTool), PreCompact (PreCompress), and SessionStart all fire. Missing UserPromptSubmit, so user decisions and corrections aren't captured — but file edits, git ops, errors, and tasks are fully tracked.
README.md:1026:**VS Code Copilot** — High coverage. Same as Gemini CLI — PostToolUse, PreCompact, and SessionStart all fire. User decisions aren't captured but all tool-level events are.
README.md:1028:**JetBrains Copilot** — High coverage. Same capabilities as VS Code Copilot — PostToolUse, PreCompact, and SessionStart all fire. Uses the same hook wire protocol and response format. User decisions aren't captured but all tool-level events are.
README.md:1030:**Cursor** — Partial coverage. Native `preToolUse` and `postToolUse` hooks capture tool events. `sessionStart` is documented by Cursor but currently rejected by their validator, so session restore is not available. Routing instructions are delivered via MCP server startup instead.
README.md:1032:**OpenCode** — Full session support. The TypeScript plugin captures PostToolUse events via `tool.execute.after`, user prompts and decisions via `chat.message`, builds compaction snapshots via `experimental.session.compacting`, and restores prior sessions via `experimental.chat.system.transform` (SessionStart surrogate). Routing block is injected on first `chat.system.transform` per session. AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/CONTEXT.md rules are captured automatically on first hook fire.
README.md:1034:**KiloCode** — Full session support. Shares the same plugin architecture as OpenCode via the OpenCodeAdapter. The TypeScript plugin captures PostToolUse events via `tool.execute.after`, user prompts and decisions via `chat.message`, builds compaction snapshots via `experimental.session.compacting`, and restores prior sessions via `experimental.chat.system.transform` (SessionStart surrogate).
README.md:1036:**OpenClaw / Pi Agent** — High coverage. All tool lifecycle hooks (`after_tool_call`, `before_compaction`, `session_start`) fire via the native gateway plugin. User decisions aren't captured but file edits, git ops, errors, and tasks are fully tracked. Falls back to DB snapshot reconstruction if compaction hooks fail on older gateway versions. See [`docs/adapters/openclaw.md`](docs/adapters/openclaw.md).
README.md:1038:**Codex CLI** — MCP active, hooks stable. Hook scripts (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop) are implemented and tested. PreToolUse deny routing works; input rewriting still depends on upstream `updatedInput` support ([openai/codex#18491](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/18491)).
README.md:1040:**Antigravity** — No session support. No hooks, no event capture. Requires manually copying `GEMINI.md` to your project root. Auto-detected via MCP protocol handshake (`clientInfo.name`).
README.md:1042:**Zed** — No session support. No hooks, no event capture. Requires manually copying `AGENTS.md` to your project root. Auto-detected via MCP protocol handshake (`clientInfo.name`).
README.md:1044:**Kiro** — Partial coverage. Native `preToolUse` and `postToolUse` hooks capture tool events and enforce sandbox routing. `agentSpawn` (the Kiro equivalent of SessionStart) is not yet implemented, so session restore after compaction is not available. Requires manually copying `KIRO.md` to your project root. Auto-detected via MCP protocol handshake (`clientInfo.name`).
README.md:1046:**Pi Coding Agent** — High coverage. The extension registers all key lifecycle events: `tool_call` (PreToolUse), `tool_result` (PostToolUse), `session_start` (SessionStart), and `session_before_compact` (PreCompact). File edits, git ops, errors, and tasks are fully tracked. Session restore after compaction works via the extension's event hooks.

README.md:1065:> **OpenCode** uses a TypeScript plugin paradigm — hooks run as in-process functions via `tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`, `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`, and `chat.message`, providing full routing enforcement, session continuity, and user-prompt capture. The `experimental.chat.system.transform` hook acts as a SessionStart surrogate to inject the routing block and restore prior sessions. The `chat.message` hook captures user prompts and decisions (UserPromptSubmit equivalent).
README.md:1067:> **KiloCode** shares the same TypeScript plugin architecture as OpenCode via the OpenCodeAdapter, with platform-specific configuration paths (`kilo.json` instead of `opencode.json`, `~/.config/kilo/` instead of `~/.config/opencode/`). Hook capabilities match OpenCode, including SessionStart surrogate via `experimental.chat.system.transform` and user-prompt capture via `chat.message`.
README.md:1069:> **OpenClaw** runs context-mode as a native gateway plugin targeting Pi Agent sessions. Hooks register via `api.on()` (tool/lifecycle) and `api.registerHook()` (commands). All tool interception and compaction hooks are supported. See [`docs/adapters/openclaw.md`](docs/adapters/openclaw.md).
README.md:1071:> **Codex CLI** hooks are stable. MCP tools work, and hook scripts activate through `~/.codex/hooks.json`. PreToolUse supports `permissionDecision: "deny"` only; input modification still needs upstream `updatedInput` support ([openai/codex#18491](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/18491)). `additionalContext` is not supported in PreToolUse (context injection works via PostToolUse and SessionStart instead; the codex formatter handles this automatically). UserPromptSubmit and Stop capture prompt and turn-end continuity events. See the Codex install section for setup. **Antigravity** and **Zed** do not support hooks. They rely solely on manually-copied routing instruction files (`AGENTS.md` / `GEMINI.md`) for enforcement (~60% compliance). See each platform's install section for copy instructions. Antigravity and Zed are auto-detected via MCP protocol handshake — no manual platform configuration needed.
README.md:1073:> **Kiro** supports native `preToolUse` and `postToolUse` hooks for routing enforcement and tool event capture. `agentSpawn` (SessionStart equivalent) and `stop` are not yet wired. Requires manually copying `KIRO.md` to your project root. Kiro is auto-detected via MCP protocol handshake (`clientInfo.name`).
README.md:1075:> **Pi Coding Agent** runs context-mode as an extension with full hook support. The extension registers `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `session_start`, and `session_before_compact` events, providing high session continuity coverage. The MCP server provides all 11 MCP tools.
README.md:1079:Hooks intercept tool calls programmatically — they can block dangerous commands and redirect them to the sandbox before execution. Instruction files guide the model via prompt instructions but cannot block anything. **Always enable hooks where supported.**
README.md:1081:> **Note:** Routing instruction files were previously auto-written to project directories on first session start. This was disabled to prevent git tree pollution ([#158](https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/issues/158), [#164](https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/issues/164)). Hook-capable platforms (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, VS Code Copilot, JetBrains Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, OpenClaw, Codex CLI) inject routing via hooks and need no file. Non-hook platforms (Zed, Kiro, Antigravity) require a one-time manual copy — see each platform's install section.

README.md:1190:Context Mode is not a CLI output filter or a cloud analytics dashboard. It operates at the MCP protocol layer — raw data stays in a sandboxed subprocess and never enters your context window. Web pages, API responses, file analysis, Playwright snapshots, log files — everything is processed in complete isolation.
README.md:1198:Context Mode enforces the same permission rules you already use — but extends them to the MCP sandbox. If you block `sudo`, it's also blocked inside `ctx_execute`, `ctx_execute_file`, and `ctx_batch_execute`.

README.md:44:Phoenix is an open-source AI observability platform designed for experimentation, evaluation, and troubleshooting. It provides:
README.md:46:- [**_Tracing_**](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/llm-traces) - Trace your LLM application's runtime using OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation.
README.md:47:- [**_Evaluation_**](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/evaluation/llm-evals) - Leverage LLMs to benchmark your application's performance using response and retrieval evals.
README.md:48:- [**_Datasets_**](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/datasets-and-experiments/overview-datasets) - Create versioned datasets of examples for experimentation, evaluation, and fine-tuning.
README.md:49:- [**_Experiments_**](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/datasets-and-experiments/overview-datasets#experiments) - Track and evaluate changes to prompts, LLMs, and retrieval.
README.md:50:- [**_Playground_**](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/prompt-engineering/overview-prompts)- Optimize prompts, compare models, adjust parameters, and replay traced LLM calls.
README.md:51:- [**_Prompt Management_**](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/prompt-engineering/overview-prompts/prompt-management)- Manage and test prompt changes systematically using version control, tagging, and experimentation.
README.md:53:Phoenix is vendor and language agnostic with out-of-the-box support for popular frameworks ([OpenAI Agents SDK](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/openai-agents-sdk), [Claude Agent SDK](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/claude-agent-sdk), [LangGraph](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/langchain), [Vercel AI SDK](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/vercel-ai-sdk), [Mastra](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/typescript/mastra), [CrewAI](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/crewai), [LlamaIndex](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/llamaindex), [DSPy](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/dspy)) and LLM providers ([OpenAI](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/openai), [Anthropic](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/anthropic), [Google GenAI](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/google-genai), [Google ADK](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/llm-providers/google-gen-ai/google-adk-tracing), [AWS Bedrock](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/bedrock), [OpenRouter](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/openrouter), [LiteLLM](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/tracing/integrations-tracing/litellm), and more). For details on auto-instrumentation, check out the [OpenInference](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference) project.

docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns.mdx:3:description: "Workflows are the backbone of many successful LLM applications. They define how language models interact with tools, data, and users—often through a sequence of clearly orchestrated steps. Unlike fully autonomous agents, workflows offer structure and predictability, making them a practical choice for many real-world tasks."
docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns.mdx:30:**Prompt Chaining** is the technique of breaking a complex task into multiple steps, where the output of one prompt becomes the input for the next. This allows a system to reason more effectively, maintain context across steps, and handle tasks that would be too difficult to solve in a single prompt. It's often used to simulate multi-step thinking or workflows.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns.mdx:40:It decides what tasks need to be done, who or what should do them, and in what order. An orchestrator can handle things like scheduling, routing, error handling, and result aggregation. It might also manage prompt chains, route tasks to agents, and oversee parallel execution.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns.mdx:44:An **evaluator** assesses the quality or correctness of outputs, such as ranking responses, checking for factual accuracy, or scoring performance against a metric. An **optimizer** uses that evaluation to improve future outputs, either by fine-tuning models, adjusting parameters, or selecting better strategies. Together, they form a feedback loop that helps a system learn what works and refine itself over time.

docs\phoenix.mdx:2:title: "What is Arize Phoenix?"
docs\phoenix.mdx:6:Phoenix helps you understand and improve AI applications by giving you a workflow for debugging and iteration. You can send detailed logging information, known as traces, from your app to see exactly what happened during a run, score outputs using evaluation tests to identify failures and regressions, iterate on your prompts using real production examples, and optimize your app with experiments that compare changes on the same inputs. Together, these tools help you move from inspecting individual runs to improving quality with evidence.
docs\phoenix.mdx:8:Phoenix is built by [Arize AI](https://www.arize.com) and the open-source community. It is built on top of OpenTelemetry and is powered by [OpenInference](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference) instrumentation. See [Integrations](/docs/phoenix/integrations) for details.
docs\phoenix.mdx:16:    <Frame caption="Tracing in Phoenix">

docs\phoenix.mdx:20:    [Tracing](/docs/phoenix/tracing/llm-traces) lets you see what happened during a single run of your AI application, step by step. A trace captures model calls, retrieval, tool use, and custom logic so you can debug behavior and understand where time is spent.
docs\phoenix.mdx:22:    Phoenix accepts traces over OpenTelemetry (OTLP) and provides [auto-instrumentation](/docs/phoenix/integrations) for popular frameworks (LlamaIndex, LangChain, DSPy, Mastra, Vercel AI SDK), providers (OpenAI, Bedrock, Anthropic), and languages (Python, TypeScript, Java).

docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns\crewai.mdx:57:Prompt chaining decomposes a complex task into a sequence of smaller steps, where each LLM call operates on the output of the previous one. This workflow introduces the ability to add programmatic checks (such as “gates”) between steps, validating intermediate outputs before continuing. The result is higher control, accuracy, and debuggability—at the cost of increased latency.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns\crewai.mdx:59:CrewAI makes it straightforward to build prompt chaining workflows using a sequential process. Each step is modeled as a `Task`, assigned to a specialized `Agent`, and executed in order using `Process.sequential`. You can insert validation logic between tasks or configure agents to flag issues before passing outputs forward.

docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns\crewai.mdx:69:In CrewAI, you implement routing by defining a Router Agent that inspects each input, emits a category label, and then dynamically delegates to downstream agents (or crews) tailored for that category—each equipped with its own tools and prompts. This separation of concerns delivers more accurate, maintainable pipelines.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns\crewai.mdx:77:Parallelization is a powerful agent workflow where multiple tasks are executed simultaneously, enabling faster and more scalable LLM pipelines. This pattern is particularly effective when tasks are independent and don’t depend on each other’s outputs.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\agent-workflow-patterns\crewai.mdx:88:The **Orchestrator-Workers** workflow centers around a primary agent—the orchestrator—that dynamically decomposes a complex task into smaller, more manageable subtasks. Rather than relying on a fixed structure or pre-defined subtasks, the orchestrator decides what needs to be done based on the input itself. It then delegates each piece to the most relevant worker agent, often specialized in a particular domain like research, content synthesis, or evaluation.

docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:14:1. Understanding Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG).
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:18:3. Evaluating RAG with Phoenix Evals.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:20:## Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:22:LLMs are trained on vast amounts of data, but these will not include your specific data (things like company knowledge bases and documentation). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this by dynamically incorporating your data as context during the generation process. This is done not by altering the training data of the LLMs but by allowing the model to access and utilize your data in real-time to provide more tailored and contextually relevant responses.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:24:In RAG, your data is loaded and prepared for queries. This process is called indexing. User queries act on this index, which filters your data down to the most relevant context. This context and your query then are sent to the LLM along with a prompt, and the LLM provides a response.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:38:* **Indexing**: This means creating a data structure that allows for querying the data. For LLMs this nearly always means creating vector embeddings, numerical representations of the meaning of your data, as well as numerous other metadata strategies to make it easy to accurately find contextually relevant data.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:42:* **Querying**: For any given indexing strategy there are many ways you can utilize LLMs and data structures to query, including sub-queries, multi-step queries, and hybrid strategies.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:48:Now that we have understood the stages of RAG, let's build a pipeline. We will use [LlamaIndex](https://www.llamaindex.ai/) for RAG and [Phoenix Evals](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/llm-evals) for evaluation.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\evaluation\evaluate-rag.mdx:72:During this tutorial, we will capture all the data we need to evaluate our RAG pipeline using Phoenix Tracing. To enable this, simply start the phoenix application and instrument LlamaIndex.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:3:description: "There are a multiple types of evaluations supported by the Phoenix Library. Each category of evaluation is categorized by its output type."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:7:  <img src="https://storage.googleapis.com/arize-assets/phoenix/assets/images/eval_types.png" alt="" />
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:10:* **Categorical (binary) -** The evaluation results in a binary output, such as true/false or yes/no, which can be easily represented as 1/0. This simplicity makes it straightforward for decision-making processes but lacks the ability to capture nuanced judgements.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:11:* **Categorical (Multi-class) -** The evaluation results in one of several predefined categories or classes, which could be text labels or distinct numbers representing different states or types.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:12:* **Score -** The evaluation results is a numeric value within a set range (e.g. 1-10), offering a scale of measurement.&#x20;
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:14:Although score evals are an option in Phoenix, we recommend using categorical evaluations in production environments. LLMs often struggle with the subtleties of continuous scales, leading to inconsistent results even with slight prompt modifications or across different models. Repeated tests have shown that scores can fluctuate significantly, which is problematic when evaluating at scale.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:16:Categorical evals, especially multi-class, strike a balance between simplicity and the ability to convey distinct evaluative outcomes, making them more suitable for applications where precise and consistent decision-making is important.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\concepts-evals\evaluation-types.mdx:18:To explore the full analysis behind our recommendation and understand the limitations of score-based evaluations, check out [our research](https://arize.com/blog-course/numeric-evals-for-llm-as-a-judge/) on LLM eval data types.

docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:18:3. Evaluating RAG with Phoenix Evals.
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:20:## Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:22:LLMs are trained on vast amounts of data, but these will not include your specific data (things like company knowledge bases and documentation). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this by dynamically incorporating your data as context during the generation process. This is done not by altering the training data of the LLMs but by allowing the model to access and utilize your data in real-time to provide more tailored and contextually relevant responses.
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:24:In RAG, your data is loaded and prepared for queries. This process is called indexing. User queries act on this index, which filters your data down to the most relevant context. This context and your query then are sent to the LLM along with a prompt, and the LLM provides a response.
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:37:* **Indexing**: This means creating a data structure that allows for querying the data. For LLMs this nearly always means creating vector embeddings, numerical representations of the meaning of your data, as well as numerous other metadata strategies to make it easy to accurately find contextually relevant data.
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:39:* **Querying**: For any given indexing strategy there are many ways you can utilize LLMs and data structures to query, including sub-queries, multi-step queries, and hybrid strategies.
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:44:Now that we have understood the stages of RAG, let's build a pipeline. We will use [LlamaIndex](https://www.llamaindex.ai/) for RAG and [Phoenix Evals](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/llm-evals) for evaluation.
docs\phoenix\use-cases\rag-evaluation.mdx:68:During this tutorial, we will capture all the data we need to evaluate our RAG pipeline using Phoenix Tracing. To enable this, simply start the phoenix application and instrument LlamaIndex.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics.mdx:3:description: "Ready-to-use evaluation metrics for measuring LLM application quality"
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics.mdx:7:Phoenix provides pre-built evaluation metrics that can be used out of the box to assess LLM application quality. These metrics are available in both Python and TypeScript and are designed to work seamlessly with Phoenix's tracing and experiment infrastructure.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics.mdx:9:All LLM evaluation templates are tested against golden datasets and achieve an F1 score of 85% or higher on benchmarks.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics.mdx:11:## LLM Evaluators
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics.mdx:13:LLM evaluators use a judge model to assess the quality of outputs. These are useful for subjective or nuanced evaluations where simple rules don't suffice.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\tutorials\customize-eval-template.mdx:26:Rather than asking an open-ended question, the prompt should act like a rubric. docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\concepts-datasets.mdx:7:Datasets are integral to evaluation and experimentation. They are collections of examples that provide the `inputs` and, optionally, expected `reference` outputs for assessing your application. Each example within a dataset represents a single data point, consisting of an `inputs` dictionary, an optional `output` dictionary, and an optional `metadata` dictionary. The `optional` output dictionary often contains the the expected LLM application output for the given input.
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\concepts-datasets.mdx:9:Datasets allow you to collect data from production, staging, evaluations, and even manually. The examples collected are then used to run experiments and evaluations to track improvements.

docs\phoenix\tracing\tutorial.mdx:3:description: "Build a fully observable AI agent from scratch - trace every operation, measure quality, and debug conversations"
docs\phoenix\tracing\tutorial.mdx:6:AI applications are fundamentally different from traditional software. A REST API returns the same response for the same input. An LLM-powered agent reasons, retrieves, calls tools, and generates - with each step influenced by probabilities, context, and the interactions between components. When something goes wrong, the failure could be anywhere in that chain.
docs\phoenix\tracing\tutorial.mdx:8:**Observability** is the practice of instrumenting your application so you can understand its internal state from its external outputs. For AI applications, this means capturing every LLM call, tool execution, retrieval operation, and generation - along with their inputs, outputs, latency, and token usage. With proper observability, you don't guess why something failed. You look at the data and see exactly what happened.
docs\phoenix\tracing\tutorial.mdx:10:Phoenix provides the infrastructure for AI observability: **tracing** to capture execution flow, **annotations** to measure quality, and **sessions** to track conversations. In this tutorial, you'll learn to use all three by building a real application.
docs\phoenix\tracing\tutorial.mdx:21:As you build each feature, you'll add the corresponding observability layer - so you can see exactly how classification decisions are made, why certain documents are retrieved, and whether conversations maintain context across turns.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics.mdx:7:Server-side evaluators run entirely in the Phoenix UI — no local code or API key setup required. Add them to any dataset from your project's Evaluators tab and Phoenix runs them automatically on every new experiment run.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics.mdx:9:There are two types of pre-built server-side evaluators:

docs\phoenix\cookbook\prompt-engineering\optimizing-coding-agent-prompts-prompt-learning.mdx:10:Coding agents are a focal point of agent development today. They are often described as the industry's most powerful agents, using state of the art LLMs, descriptive and effective tools, and carefully crafted architectures. Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, etc. tend to use one large system prompt for the entire application. Since this prompt plays a huge role in the execution of the agent, rule files are offered - where the user can write down a custom set of instructions to be appended to the system prompt. Developers spend time thinking about writing good rules so their coding agents can perform better.

docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\repetitions.mdx:11:Since LLMs are probabilistic, their synthesis can differ even when the supplied prompts are exactly the same. This can make it challenging to determine if a particular change is warranted as a single execution cannot concretely tell you whether a given change improves or degrades your task.
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\repetitions.mdx:17:Repetitions can be configured whenever you run an experiment via the phoenix client. The **repetitions** parameter determines how many times each **example** is used in your task. So if you have 3 examples with 2 repetitions, your task will be run 6 times and evaluated 6 times.
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\repetitions.mdx:57:If you've run your experiments with repetitions, you will see arrow icons at the top of each output. At the bottom you will see the average of the evaluations as well as the score for the evaluation you are looking at. You can click on the arrows to cycle through the repetitions or click on the expand icon to view the full details.
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\splits.mdx:14:* a split of examples used in a few-shot prompt and a disjoint, non-overlapping split of examples used for evaluation,

docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\splits.mdx:17:Running experiments over splits rather than entire datasets produces evaluation metrics that better capture the performance of your agent, workflow, or prompt on the particular type of data you care about.
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\splits.mdx:21:Experiments can be run over previously configured splits either via the Python or JavaScript clients or via the Phoenix playground.
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\splits.mdx:106:Splits are implicitly configured when a dataset is pulled from the Phoenix server using the `get_dataset` client method. Subsequent invocations of `run_experiment` only run on the examples belonging to the split(s).
docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\splits.mdx:131:Splits can be configured within a DatasetSelector, when fetching datasets. Dataset examples contained within the selected splits will be used in experiment runs, or evaluations.

docs\phoenix\cookbook\prompt-engineering\llm-as-a-judge-prompt-optimization.mdx:2:title: "LLM-as-a-Judge Prompt Optimization"
docs\phoenix\cookbook\prompt-engineering\llm-as-a-judge-prompt-optimization.mdx:9:## LLM as a Judge
docs\phoenix\cookbook\prompt-engineering\llm-as-a-judge-prompt-optimization.mdx:11:An LLM as a Judge refers to using an LLM as a tool for evaluating and scoring responses based on predefined criteria.
docs\phoenix\cookbook\prompt-engineering\llm-as-a-judge-prompt-optimization.mdx:13:While LLMs are powerful tools for evaluation, their performance can be inconsistent. Factors like ambiguity in the prompt, biases in the model, or a lack of clear guidelines can lead to unreliable results. docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:3:description: "Evaluate whether LLMs select the correct tools for given tasks"
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:8:The **Tool Selection** evaluator determines whether an LLM selected the most appropriate tool (or tools) for a given task. This evaluator focuses on the *what* of tool calling - validating that the right tool was chosen - rather than whether the invocation arguments were correct.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:12:Use the Tool Selection evaluator when you need to:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:14:- **Validate tool choice decisions** - Ensure the LLM picks the most appropriate tool for the task
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:15:- **Detect hallucinated tools** - Identify when the LLM tries to use tools that don't exist
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:16:- **Evaluate tool necessity** - Check if the LLM correctly determines when tools are (or aren't) needed
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:17:- **Assess multi-tool selection** - Validate when the LLM needs to select multiple tools for complex tasks
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:20:This evaluator validates tool selection correctness, not invocation correctness. For evaluating whether tool arguments are properly formatted, use the [Tool Invocation evaluator](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/pre-built-metrics/tool-invocation) instead. The two evaluators are complementary — Tool Selection catches wrong-tool errors while Tool Invocation catches malformed-call errors — and are best run together for complete tool-calling coverage.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:25:The level of an evaluator determines the scope of the evaluation in OpenTelemetry terms. Some evaluations are applicable to individual spans, some to full traces or sessions, and some are applicable at multiple levels.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:29:| **Span** | Yes | Best for LLM spans that contain tool calls. Evaluate individual tool selection decisions. |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:31:**Relevant span kinds:** LLM spans with tool calls, particularly in agentic applications.

docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\run-experiments-in-background.mdx:10:Experiments that iterate over large datasets or call slow models can take a while. Tying them to a browser tab is fragile — close the laptop, lose the work. When you run an experiment from the Phoenix Playground, Phoenix executes it on the server as a **background job**, so you can close the tab, navigate away, or even restart the server and the experiment keeps going until every example has been evaluated.

docs\phoenix\datasets-and-experiments\how-to-experiments\run-experiments-in-background.mdx:30:| `ERROR` | The job was halted by the server after repeated failures from the LLM provider. Can be resumed once the issue is addressed. |

docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-response-handling.mdx:8:The **Tool Response Handling** evaluator determines whether an AI agent correctly processed a tool's result to produce an appropriate output. This evaluator focuses on the *what happens after* the tool calling — validating that the agent used the tool result accurately — rather than whether the right tool was selected or invoked correctly.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-response-handling.mdx:12:Use the Tool Response Handling evaluator when you need to:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-response-handling.mdx:21:This evaluator validates how the agent handled the tool result, not whether the right tool was chosen or invoked correctly. Use the [Tool Selection evaluator](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/pre-built-metrics/tool-selection) to evaluate tool choice, and the [Tool Invocation evaluator](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/pre-built-metrics/tool-invocation) to validate argument correctness. Together, all three evaluators provide complete coverage of the tool-calling pipeline.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\tool-response-handling.mdx:26:The level of an evaluator determines the scope of the evaluation in OpenTelemetry terms. Some evaluations are applicable to individual spans, some to full traces or sessions, and some are applicable at multiple levels.

Evaluations give you a systematic way to catch regressions, compare model or prompt changes, and build confidence before shipping.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:3:description: "Evaluate whether LLM responses are faithful to the provided context."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:8:The **Faithfulness** evaluator is a specialized hallucination-detection metric that determines whether an LLM's response is grounded in and faithful to the provided context. It detects when responses contain information that is not supported by or contradicts the reference context.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:12:Use the Faithfulness evaluator when you need to:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:14:- **Validate RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) outputs** - Ensure answers are based on retrieved documents or search results
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:15:- **Detect hallucinations in grounded responses** - Identify when the LLM makes up information not present in the context
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:19:This evaluator is specifically designed for **grounded** responses where context is provided. It is not designed to validate general world knowledge or facts the LLM learned during training.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:24:The level of an evaluator determines the scope of the evaluation in OpenTelemetry terms. Some evaluations are applicable to individual spans, some to full traces or sessions, and some are applicable at multiple levels.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:28:| **Span** | Yes | Best for LLM spans with RAG context. Apply to spans where `input`, `output`, and retrieved `context` are available. |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:30:**Relevant span kinds:** LLM spans, particularly those in RAG pipelines where documents are retrieved and used as context.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:34:The Faithfulness evaluator requires three inputs:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\faithfulness.mdx:39:| `output` | `string` | The LLM's response to evaluate |

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:3:description: "Evaluate whether LLMs select the correct tools for given tasks using a Phoenix-managed judge model."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:8:The **Tool Selection** evaluator determines whether an LLM selected the most appropriate tool (or tools) for a given task. This evaluator focuses on the *what* of tool calling — validating that the right tool was chosen — rather than whether the invocation arguments were correct.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:10:This is an LLM evaluator: Phoenix runs a judge model against a managed prompt template on your behalf.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:14:Use the Tool Selection evaluator when you need to:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:16:- **Validate tool choice decisions** — Ensure the LLM picks the most appropriate tool for the task
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:17:- **Detect hallucinated tools** — Identify when the LLM tries to use tools that don't exist
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:18:- **Evaluate tool necessity** — Check if the LLM correctly determines when tools are (or aren't) needed
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:19:- **Assess multi-tool selection** — Validate when the LLM needs to select multiple tools for complex tasks
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-selection.mdx:22:This evaluator validates tool selection correctness, not invocation correctness. For evaluating whether tool arguments are properly formatted, use the [Tool Invocation evaluator](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/server-evals/pre-built-metrics/tool-invocation) instead. The two evaluators are complementary — Tool Selection catches wrong-tool errors while Tool Invocation catches malformed-call errors — and are best run together for complete tool-calling coverage.

This evaluator focuses on the *how* of tool calling — validating that the invocation itself is well-formed — rather than whether the right tool was selected.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\tool-invocation.mdx:23:This evaluator validates tool invocation correctness, not tool selection. For evaluating whether the right tool was chosen, use the [Tool Selection evaluator](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/server-evals/pre-built-metrics/tool-selection) instead. docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:3:description: Tracing the execution of LLM applications using Telemetry
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:7:Phoenix traces AI applications, via OpenTelemetry and has first-class integrations with LlamaIndex, LangChain, OpenAI, and others.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:9:LLM tracing records the paths taken by requests as they propagate through multiple steps or components of an LLM application. For example, when a user interacts with an LLM application, tracing can capture the sequence of operations, such as document retrieval, embedding generation, language model invocation, and response generation to provide a detailed timeline of the request's execution.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:11:Tracing is a helpful tool for understanding how your LLM application works. Phoenix offers comprehensive tracing capabilities that are not tied to any specific LLM vendor or framework. Phoenix accepts traces over the OpenTelemetry protocol (OTLP) and supports first-class instrumentation for a variety of frameworks ( [LlamaIndex](/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/llamaindex), [LangChain](/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/langchain), [DSPy](/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/dspy/dspy-tracing)), SDKs ([OpenAI](/docs/phoenix/integrations/llm-providers/openai), [Bedrock](/docs/phoenix/integrations/llm-providers/amazon-bedrock), [Mistral](/docs/phoenix/integrations/llm-providers/mistralai), [Vertex](/docs/phoenix/integrations/llm-providers/vertexai)), and languages. ([Python](/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/agno), [TypeScript](/docs/phoenix/integrations/typescript/beeai), etc.)
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:13:<Frame caption="View the inner workings for your LLM Application">
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:17:Using Phoenix's tracing capabilities can provide important insights into the inner workings of your LLM application. By analyzing the collected trace data, you can identify and address various performance and operational issues and improve the overall reliability and efficiency of your system.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:19:* **Application Latency**: Identify and address slow invocations of LLMs, Retrievers, and other components within your application, enabling you to optimize performance and responsiveness.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:21:* **Token Usage**: Gain a detailed breakdown of token usage for your LLM calls, allowing you to identify and optimize the most expensive LLM invocations.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:25:* **Retrieved Documents**: Inspect the documents retrieved during a Retriever call, including the score and order in which they were returned to provide insight into the retrieval process.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:27:* **Embeddings**: Examine the embedding text used for retrieval and the underlying embedding model to allow you to validate and refine your embedding strategies.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:29:* **LLM Parameters**: Inspect the parameters used when calling an LLM, such as temperature and system prompts, to ensure optimal configuration and debugging.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:31:* **Prompt Templates**: Understand the prompt templates used during the prompting step and the variables that were applied, allowing you to fine-tune and improve your prompting strategies.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:33:* **Tool Descriptions**: View the descriptions and function signatures of the tools your LLM has been given access to in order to better understand and control your LLM’s capabilities.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:35:* **LLM Function Calls**: For LLMs with function call capabilities (e.g., OpenAI), you can inspect the function selection and function messages in the input to the LLM, further improving your ability to debug and optimize your application.
docs\phoenix\tracing\llm-traces.mdx:37:By using tracing in Phoenix, you can gain increased visibility into your LLM application, empowering you to identify and address performance bottlenecks, optimize resource utilization, and ensure the overall reliability and effectiveness of your system.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:3:description: "Detect when an LLM refuses or declines to answer a user query."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:8:The **Refusal** evaluator detects when an LLM refuses, declines, or avoids answering a user query. It captures explicit refusals, scope disclaimers, lack-of-information responses, safety refusals, redirections, and apologetic non-answers.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:12:Use the Refusal evaluator when you need to:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:15:- **Flag scope disclaimers** - Catch responses claiming the question is outside the LLM's responsibilities
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:18:- **Monitor refusal rates** - Track how often your LLM declines to engage with user queries
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:21:The Refusal evaluator is use-case agnostic. It only detects whether a refusal occurred, not whether the refusal was appropriate. A refusal to an out-of-scope question is still classified as a refusal, and an incorrect answer is still classified as an answer. Use it alongside other evaluators like [Correctness](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/pre-built-metrics/correctness) to get a complete picture.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:26:The level of an evaluator determines the scope of the evaluation in OpenTelemetry terms. Some evaluations are applicable to individual spans, some to full traces or sessions, and some are applicable at multiple levels.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:30:| **Span** | Yes | Apply to LLM spans to detect refusals in individual responses. |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:32:**Relevant span kinds:** LLM spans, particularly in conversational or retrieval-augmented systems.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:36:The Refusal evaluator requires two inputs:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:41:| `output` | `string` | The LLM's response to evaluate |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:57:The evaluator returns a `Score` object with the following properties:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:63:| `explanation` | `string` | LLM-generated reasoning for the classification |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:65:| `metadata` | `object` | Additional information such as the model name. When tracing is enabled, includes the `trace_id` for the evaluation. |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:68:- **Refused (1.0)**: The LLM declined, deflected, or avoided answering the query
docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\refusal.mdx:69:- **Answered (0.0)**: The LLM provided a substantive response, regardless of correctness or quality

docs\phoenix\cookbook\ai-engineering-workflows\analyzing-customer-review-evals-with-repetition-experiments.mdx:6:Large Language Models (LLMs) are probabilistic; the same prompt can yield different outputs across runs. docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\levenshtein-distance.mdx:31:**Answer closeness** — A QA model where small paraphrasing is acceptable but significant divergence is not. **Actual** receives the model's text response; **Expected** receives the reference answer from your dataset, typically a path like `reference.answer`. Comparing average edit distance across experiment runs shows whether prompt changes are moving outputs closer to reference.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\levenshtein-distance.mdx:33:**Entity extraction quality** — A pipeline that extracts a specific named value (a product name, location, or identifier). **Actual** is the extracted value from the model's output — often a nested path like `output.entity` if the response is structured JSON. **Expected** is the ground-truth value per example in your dataset. Edit distance reveals whether extraction is improving as you iterate on prompts or model configuration.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\levenshtein-distance.mdx:35:**Comparative prompt evaluation** — Two prompt variants tested against the same dataset. **Actual** receives the response field from each run; **Expected** stays fixed, pointing to the same reference column. The variant with the lower average Levenshtein score is closer to the reference outputs.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\pre-built-metrics\levenshtein-distance.mdx:40:The algorithm runs in O(n×m) time, where n and m are the lengths of the two strings. Performance degrades quadratically on very long inputs. Keep inputs under a few thousand characters for predictable evaluation times.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:2:title: "LLM Evaluators"
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:3:description: "LLM-as-a-judge evaluators that use Phoenix-managed prompts to label and score experiment outputs with full version control and traceability."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:6:LLM evaluators use a language model to label and score experiment outputs. You write a prompt that describes your evaluation criteria, attach it to a dataset, and Phoenix handles the rest — formatting inputs, calling the model, and parsing structured labels and scores from the response.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:8:Because LLM evaluators are backed by Phoenix's prompt management system, every change to your evaluation criteria is versioned. You can iterate on a prompt, tag a known-good version, and have your evaluator pin to that version while you continue experimenting.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:14:Every LLM evaluator is backed by a Phoenix prompt. When you create an LLM evaluator, Phoenix either creates a new prompt or links to an existing one. The prompt template defines how your evaluation parameters — the model's input, output, reference data, and metadata — are presented to the judge.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:16:Templates use Mustache syntax. Variables like `{{output}}` and `{{reference}}` are replaced at evaluation time with values drawn from the evaluation parameters via [input mapping](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/server-evals/input-mapping).
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:18:A typical evaluator prompt has two parts:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:20:- **System message** — Describes the evaluator's persona, the scoring rubric, and any grading instructions.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:21:- **User message** — Presents the data to evaluate, using template variables that get filled from the evaluation parameters.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:25:You are an expert at evaluating whether a model's response
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:57:The output config defines what the evaluator produces. It becomes a tool that the LLM calls to return its judgment as structured output, ensuring labels and scores are always in the expected format.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:70:LLM evaluators inherit their model configuration from the prompt. docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:72:See [Configure AI Providers](/docs/phoenix/prompt-engineering/how-to-prompts/configure-ai-providers) for the full list of supported providers, credential setup, and custom provider configuration.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:76:Evaluation quality depends heavily on prompt quality, and prompt quality improves through iteration. Phoenix tracks every version of an evaluator's prompt so you can see exactly which criteria produced a given set of labels and scores.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:80:Each time you save changes to an evaluator's prompt — whether updating the template text, switching models, or adjusting invocation parameters — Phoenix creates a new prompt version. Previous versions are preserved and can be viewed on the prompt's **Versions** tab.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:83:  ![Prompt version history](https://storage.googleapis.com/arize-phoenix-assets/assets/images/evaluator-prompt-version-history.png)
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:88:Every LLM evaluator has a **prompt version tag** that determines which version of the prompt is used at evaluation time. This tag is a named pointer within Phoenix's prompt management system. When you create an evaluator, Phoenix auto-generates a tag named after the evaluator (e.g. `correctness-evaluator-932646b7`).
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:92:1. **Create an evaluator** — Phoenix creates a prompt and a tag pointing to the initial version.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:93:2. **Iterate** — Edit the prompt in the playground, test it against sample data, and compare versions.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:94:3. **Promote** — When satisfied, save the prompt and advance the tag. The evaluator now uses the new version.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\llm-evaluators.mdx:96:When you click **Save Prompt** in the playground, a modal shows checkboxes for available tags. To advance the evaluator's tag to the new version, **check the tag that starts with the evaluator's name** (e.g. `correctness-evaluator-932646b7`). If you leave it unchecked, the new version is saved but the evaluator continues using the previously tagged version.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\pre-built-metrics\conciseness.mdx:8:The **Conciseness** evaluator assesses whether an LLM's response uses the minimum number of words necessary to fully answer the question. docs\phoenix\evaluation\how-to-evals\custom-llm-evaluators.mdx:115:**Note**: We generally recommend using categorical labels over numeric ratings for most evaluation tasks. LLMs have inherent limitations in their numeric reasoning abilities, and numeric scores do not correlate as well with human judgements. See this [technical report](https://arize.com/blog/testing-binary-vs-score-llm-evals-on-the-latest-models/) for more information about our findings on this subject.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:3:description: "Control how dataset and task output values flow into evaluator inputs using JSONPath expressions and literal values."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:6:When you associate an evaluator with a dataset, input mapping defines how data reaches the evaluator's parameters. Evaluators have an input schema — a set of named parameters they expect — and input mapping is how you connect those parameters to values from your experiments.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:8:This decoupling is what makes evaluators reusable. The same evaluator can work across datasets with different column structures because the mapping layer adapts the data shape at evaluation time.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:12:Every time an evaluator runs, it receives **evaluation parameters** — a dictionary with four top-level keys built from the dataset example and the task output:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:21:Input mapping extracts values from these parameters and passes them to the evaluator's inputs.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:24:In the future, when server evals extend to incoming traces, the evaluation parameters will be constructed from span and trace attributes rather than dataset examples — but the mapping mechanism will work the same way.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:29:Each evaluator parameter can be mapped in one of two modes, toggled inline in the UI next to each field.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:33:Path mapping uses [JSONPath](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9535) expressions to extract values from the evaluation parameters. This is the right choice when the evaluator input should come from your data — a model response, a reference answer, a metadata field.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:35:Paths are evaluated against the full parameter dictionary. Common patterns:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:45:| `output['trace-id']` | A field whose name contains special characters |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:47:The Phoenix UI provides a searchable dropdown of paths auto-generated from your dataset's columns, but you can type any valid JSONPath expression directly.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:50:If a JSONPath expression matches nothing in the evaluation parameters, the evaluation fails with an error rather than silently passing `null`. Double-check that your paths match the actual structure of your dataset and task outputs.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:66:If no explicit mapping is provided for a parameter, Phoenix falls back to matching by name. docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:68:This means for simple cases — where your evaluator parameters are named `input`, `output`, `reference`, or `metadata` — you don't need to configure any mapping at all. The defaults connect things correctly.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:72:Phoenix resolves each evaluator parameter in the following order:
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:74:1. **Path mapping** — If a JSONPath expression is defined for the parameter, evaluate it against the evaluation parameters.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:76:3. **Name fallback** — If neither mapping is defined and the parameter name matches a top-level key in the evaluation parameters, use that value directly.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\input-mapping.mdx:78:After resolution, the values are validated against the evaluator's input schema. String-typed parameters receive automatic type coercion (non-string values are converted to their string representation), but structural mismatches raise an error.

docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:3:description: "Server-side code evaluators that label and score experiment outputs without requiring an LLM, API keys, or any installation."
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:6:Built-in evaluators run server-side and are always available to add to any dataset. Configure them in the Phoenix UI and they label and score each output automatically when an experiment runs.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:22:Each evaluator parameter can be set to either a **path** (a JSONPath expression that extracts a value from the evaluation parameters) or a **literal** (a fixed value typed directly). Use paths to pull from dataset inputs, task outputs, reference data, or metadata. Use literals for static configuration like regex patterns or word lists.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:24:See [Input Mapping](/docs/phoenix/evaluation/server-evals/input-mapping) for full details on mapping modes, resolution order, and examples.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:60:If `words` is empty or contains only whitespace after splitting on commas, the evaluator returns `false` rather than `true`. This guards against the empty-list edge case where "all of nothing" would otherwise trivially pass.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:74:| `actual` | string | Yes | — | The value to evaluate |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:144:| `actual` | string | Yes | — | The string to evaluate |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:156:**Answer closeness** — A QA model where small paraphrasing is acceptable but significant divergence is not. **Actual** receives the model's text response; **Expected** receives the reference answer from your dataset, typically a path like `reference.answer`. Comparing average edit distance across experiment runs shows whether prompt changes are moving outputs closer to reference.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:158:**Entity extraction quality** — A pipeline that extracts a specific named value (a product name, location, or identifier). **Actual** is the extracted value from the model's output — often a nested path like `output.entity` if the response is structured JSON. **Expected** is the ground-truth value per example in your dataset. Edit distance reveals whether extraction is improving as you iterate on prompts or model configuration.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:160:**Comparative prompt evaluation** — Two prompt variants tested against the same dataset. **Actual** receives the response field from each run; **Expected** stays fixed, pointing to the same reference column. The variant with the lower average Levenshtein score is closer to the reference outputs.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:165:The algorithm runs in O(n×m) time, where n and m are the lengths of the two strings. Performance degrades quadratically on very long inputs. Keep inputs under a few thousand characters for predictable evaluation times.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:181:| `actual` | any | Yes | — | The JSON structure to evaluate |
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:197:**Prompt change regression tracking** — Running the same dataset against two different prompt versions. **Actual** receives the JSON output from each run; **Expected** stays fixed, pointing to the reference JSON in your dataset. Comparing average distance across runs reveals whether a prompt change introduced new structural errors.
docs\phoenix\evaluation\server-evals\builtin-evaluators.mdx:202:If either input cannot be parsed as JSON (when `parse_strings` is `true`), the evaluator returns a `null` score with an error explanation rather than a numeric result. Ensure your dataset fields contain valid JSON strings when using this evaluator with path mappings.

docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:42:This guide walks through a complete workflow for understanding and improving an agent application using Phoenix.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:50:- An application instrumented with tracing so you can see how requests execute
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:54:- A way to iterate on prompts and logic and verify whether those changes help
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:64:A trace is a record of a single run of your application, broken down into spans that show what happened at each step. In this guide, you instrument an application and send trace data to Phoenix. Traces show how agents, tasks, and tools executed during a run, and provide the raw data needed for everything that follows.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:72:An evaluation produces a score or label for an output, so you can track quality across runs. In this guide, you define evaluations and run them on existing trace data. Evaluations attach quality signals to runs so that correctness or relevance can be reasoned about consistently instead of judged case by case.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:74:This turns traces from observations into something you can measure.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:80:A prompt is the set of instructions and context sent to the model to produce an output. In this guide, you start from real prompts captured during executions, group failing runs into a dataset, and use the Prompt Playground to iterate on prompt variants. Prompt Hub is used to save and reuse prompts across runs.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:82:This lets you evaluate prompt changes using the same data and criteria instead of relying on spot checks.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:88:An experiment is a structured comparison between versions of your application using the same inputs and evaluation criteria. In this guide, you pull down an existing dataset and run experiments in code to compare different versions of your application using the same inputs and evaluation criteria. This makes it possible to test changes and verify whether they actually improve quality.
docs\phoenix\get-started.mdx:94:If you are new to Phoenix, start with either [Python: Get Started with Tracing](/docs/phoenix/get-started/get-started-tracing) or [TypeScript: Get Started with Tracing](/docs/phoenix/get-started/ts-get-started-tracing) and follow the guides in order.
