docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:2:title: "01.18.2025: Automatic & manual span tracing"
docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:3:description: Available in Phoenix 7.9+
docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:19:In addition to using our automatic instrumentors and tracing directly using OTEL, we've now added our own layer to let you have the granularity of manual instrumentation without as much boilerplate code.
docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:21:You can now access a tracer object with streamlined options to trace functions and code blocks. The main two options are:
docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:23:* Using the **decorator** `@tracer.chain` traces the entire function automatically as a Span in Phoenix. The input, output, and status attributes are set based on the function's parameters and return value.
docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:24:* Using the tracer in a `with` clause allows you to trace specific code blocks within a function. You manually define the Span name, input, output, and status.
docs\phoenix\release-notes\01-2025\01-18-2025-automatic-and-manual-span-tracing.mdx:26:Check out the [docs](/docs/phoenix/tracing/how-to-tracing/setup-tracing/instrument-python#using-your-tracer) for more on how to use tracer objects.

docs\sdk-watcher.md:3:The SDK service exposes a watcher integration that surfaces granular auth updates without forcing a full reload. This document explains the queue contract, how the service consumes updates, and how high-frequency change bursts are handled.
docs\sdk-watcher.md:7:- `watcher.AuthUpdate` represents a single credential change. `Action` may be `add`, `modify`, or `delete`, and `ID` carries the credential identifier. For `add`/`modify` the `Auth` payload contains a fully populated clone of the credential; `delete` may omit `Auth`.
docs\sdk-watcher.md:23:- If the queue is saturated for an extended period, updates continue to be merged, so the latest state is eventually applied without replaying redundant intermediate states.

skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:756:### Develop Skills iteratively with Claude
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:758:The most effective Skill development process involves Claude itself. Work with one instance of Claude ("Claude A") to create a Skill that will be used by other instances ("Claude B"). Claude A helps you design and refine instructions, while Claude B tests them in real tasks. This works because Claude models understand both how to write effective agent instructions and what information agents need.
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:760:**Creating a new Skill:**
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:762:1. **Complete a task without a Skill**: Work through a problem with Claude A using normal prompting. As you work, you'll naturally provide context, explain preferences, and share procedural knowledge. Notice what information you repeatedly provide.
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:768:3. **Ask Claude A to create a Skill**: "Create a Skill that captures this BigQuery analysis pattern we just used. Include the table schemas, naming conventions, and the rule about filtering test accounts."
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:771:     Claude models understand the Skill format and structure natively. You don't need special system prompts or a "writing skills" skill to get Claude to help create Skills. Simply ask Claude to create a Skill and it will generate properly structured SKILL.md content with appropriate frontmatter and body content.
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:778:6. **Test on similar tasks**: Use the Skill with Claude B (a fresh instance with the Skill loaded) on related use cases. Observe whether Claude B finds the right information, applies rules correctly, and handles the task successfully.
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:780:7. **Iterate based on observation**: If Claude B struggles or misses something, return to Claude A with specifics: "When Claude used this Skill, it forgot to filter by date for Q4. Should we add a section about date filtering patterns?"
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:782:**Iterating on existing Skills:**
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:784:The same hierarchical pattern continues when improving Skills. You alternate between:
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:786:* **Working with Claude A** (the expert who helps refine the Skill)
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:787:* **Testing with Claude B** (the agent using the Skill to perform real work)
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:790:1. **Use the Skill in real workflows**: Give Claude B (with the Skill loaded) actual tasks, not test scenarios
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:794:   **Example observation**: "When I asked Claude B for a regional sales report, it wrote the query but forgot to filter out test accounts, even though the Skill mentions this rule."
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:796:3. **Return to Claude A for improvements**: Share the current SKILL.md and describe what you observed. Ask: "I noticed Claude B forgot to filter test accounts when I asked for a regional report. The Skill mentions filtering, but maybe it's not prominent enough?"
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:800:5. **Apply and test changes**: Update the Skill with Claude A's refinements, then test again with Claude B on similar requests
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:802:6. **Repeat based on usage**: Continue this observe-refine-test cycle as you encounter new scenarios. Each iteration improves the Skill based on real agent behavior, not assumptions.
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:806:1. Share Skills with teammates and observe their usage
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:807:2. Ask: Does the Skill activate when expected? Are instructions clear? What's missing?
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:810:**Why this approach works**: Claude A understands agent needs, you provide domain expertise, Claude B reveals gaps through real usage, and iterative refinement improves Skills based on observed behavior rather than assumptions.
skills\writing-skills\anthropic-best-practices.md:812:### Observe how Claude navigates Skills

README.md:3:An agent you can leave running for hours needs more than a good prompt. It needs a small amount of structure around it: enforcement that "done" means observed evidence, an independent check on its own claims, and a way for the next session to pick up cleanly where this one left off. [Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) (Nov 2025) and [Harness Design for Long-Running Application Development](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps) (Mar 2026) describe these patterns; this repo is the code companion. It ships a short, readable example of each as a native [Claude Code hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) or subagent, so you can see the mechanism, copy what fits, and wire it into your own harness.
README.md:7:- **Default-FAIL contract.** Every criterion starts `false`; the agent can't mark it passing without opening evidence first.
README.md:8:- **Fresh-context evaluator.** A separate agent with no Write/Edit tools grades the work from a context window that never saw the build.

README.md:42:### Default-FAIL contract
README.md:44:Agents will mark a feature "passing" after a unit test or a curl when the UI is visibly broken. Asking nicely in the prompt doesn't reliably stop this. The harness makes "done" structural. Every feature is a row in a `test-results.json` file you create in your project:
README.md:52:### Fresh-context evaluator
README.md:54:The builder shouldn't grade its own work. After each feature, you (or your wrapper script) invoke a separate subagent (`agents/evaluator.md`) with no Write/Edit tools that reviews the diff and the screenshots from a context window that never saw the build, then returns `PASS` or `NEEDS_WORK` with specific findings. On `NEEDS_WORK` the findings become the next builder session's starting prompt, closing the build/evaluate/rebuild loop. Invoke it from your wrapper with `claude --agent evaluator -p "<review prompt>"`; what your loop does with the verdict is up to you.
README.md:58:A fresh session has no memory of what the previous one did, and when a long session fills its context window Claude Code summarizes the history, which loses detail. So the agent maintains the handoff itself: it scopes each session to one feature, writes to a structured `PROGRESS.md` as it works and re-reads it first thing on every restart, and `git add`s and commits at meaningful checkpoints so `git log` is a second record. `commit-on-stop.sh` is the backstop that catches whatever's still uncommitted at session end. This is the layer most sensitive to model capability; newer models drift less and self-scope better, so re-evaluate how much of `CLAUDE.md` you still need after each model release (see [Re-simplify on model upgrades](#going-further)).
README.md:60:A fourth core piece, a **rubric for subjective work**, isn't shipped here because it's project-specific; see [Going further](#going-further) for how to add one to the evaluator.
README.md:64:Two more hooks for when you want to watch the loop run or intervene mid-stream. These aren't part of the quality story; they're how a human stays in the loop.

claude-code-config\README.md:1:# Claude Code config: long-running primitives
claude-code-config\README.md:3:Example implementations of the long-running primitives as native Claude Code hooks. Copy `.claude/` into your project as a starting point and adapt the file paths and matching rules to fit.
claude-code-config\README.md:5:**Requires:** `bash`, `git`, `python3` (the hooks parse JSON via python3; without it they silently no-op).
claude-code-config\README.md:9:chmod +x /path/to/your/project/.claude/hooks/*.sh
claude-code-config\README.md:15:| `.claude/hooks/kill-switch.sh` | Halt every tool call while `./AGENT_STOP` exists |
claude-code-config\README.md:16:| `.claude/hooks/steer.sh` | Surface `./STEER.md` content to the agent once, then clear it |
claude-code-config\README.md:17:| `.claude/hooks/track-read.sh` + `verify-gate.sh` | Deny marking a test passing until evidence (screenshot/console log) has been Read |
claude-code-config\README.md:18:| `.claude/hooks/commit-on-stop.sh` | Commit at the end of every session |

docs\install-provenance.md:4797:The plugin's `cli.bundle.mjs` ctx_doctor implementation tries `spawn('bun', ...)` to verify the Bun runtime is available. On Windows, Node's `child_process.spawn` doesn't auto-resolve `.cmd` shims unless `shell: true` — and `npm install -g bun` creates `bun.cmd` shim, not `bun.exe`. Solution: install via official bun.sh installer which produces real `bun.exe`.

So bun.exe landed at `Z:/claude-sota-installed/.bun/bin/bun.exe` instead of `~/.bun/bin/`. The shell PATH already had `/c/Users/42/.bun/bin` — copied bun.exe there for ctx_doctor's spawn-discoverable path.

README.en.md:5:CPA Usage Keeper is a standalone CPA usage persistence and dashboard service.
README.en.md:7:It relies on [CLIProxyAPI (CPA)](https://github.com/router-for-me/CLIProxyAPI) as the backend CPA data source and adds persistent storage and statistical analysis capabilities on top of CPA. The service consumes events from the CPA Redis usage queue into SQLite, periodically pulls CPA metadata, exposes aggregation APIs, and serves a built-in web dashboard for usage, pricing, request health, and model/API statistics.

README.en.md:174:sudo systemctl enable --now cpa-usage-keeper # Enable startup on boot and start the service now.
README.en.md:180:sudo systemctl status cpa-usage-keeper # Show service status.
README.en.md:181:sudo journalctl -u cpa-usage-keeper -f # Follow service logs.

README.md:209:## How Skills Work
README.md:219:│  │ description: Guides agents through [task].│  │
README.md:233:- **Process, not prose.** Skills are workflows agents follow, not reference docs they read. Each has steps, checkpoints, and exit criteria.
README.md:234:- **Anti-rationalization.** Every skill includes a table of common excuses agents use to skip steps (e.g., "I'll add tests later") with documented counter-arguments.

README.md:276:## Why Agent Skills?
README.md:278:AI coding agents default to the shortest path - which often means skipping specs, tests, security reviews, and the practices that make software reliable. Agent Skills gives agents structured workflows that enforce the same discipline senior engineers bring to production code.
README.md:282:Skills bake in best practices from Google's engineering culture — including concepts from [Software Engineering at Google](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book) and Google's [engineering practices guide](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/). You'll find Hyrum's Law in API design, the Beyonce Rule and test pyramid in testing, change sizing and review speed norms in code review, Chesterton's Fence in simplification, trunk-based development in git workflow, Shift Left and feature flags in CI/CD, and a dedicated deprecation skill treating code as a liability. These aren't abstract principles — they're embedded directly into the step-by-step workflows agents follow.
README.md:288:Skills should be **specific** (actionable steps, not vague advice), **verifiable** (clear exit criteria with evidence requirements), **battle-tested** (based on real workflows), and **minimal** (only what's needed to guide the agent).
README.md:296:MIT - use these skills in your projects, teams, and tools.

skills\deprecation-and-migration\SKILL.md:10:Code is a liability, not an asset. Every line of code has ongoing maintenance cost — bugs to fix, dependencies to update, security patches to apply, and new engineers to onboard. Deprecation is the discipline of removing code that no longer earns its keep, and migration is the process of moving users safely from the old to the new.
skills\deprecation-and-migration\SKILL.md:20:- Planning the lifecycle of a new system (deprecation planning starts at design time)
skills\deprecation-and-migration\SKILL.md:27:Every line of code has ongoing cost: it needs tests, documentation, security patches, dependency updates, and mental overhead for anyone working nearby. The value of code is the functionality it provides, not the code itself. When the same functionality can be provided with less code, less complexity, or better abstractions — the old code should go.

README.md:192:### Reliable Routing
README.md:193:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-37">**Fallbacks**</a>: Fallback to another provider or model on failed requests using the LLM gateway. You can specify the errors on which to trigger the fallback. Improves reliability of your application.
README.md:194:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-38">**Automatic Retries**</a>: Automatically retry failed requests up to 5 times. An exponential backoff strategy spaces out retry attempts to prevent network overload.
README.md:195:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-39">**Load Balancing**</a>: Distribute LLM requests across multiple API keys or AI providers with weights to ensure high availability and optimal performance.
README.md:196:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-40">**Request Timeouts**</a>: Manage unruly LLMs & latencies by setting up granular request timeouts, allowing automatic termination of requests that exceed a specified duration.
README.md:197:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-41">**Multi-modal LLM Gateway**</a>: Call vision, audio (text-to-speech & speech-to-text), and image generation models from multiple providers  — all using the familiar OpenAI signature
README.md:198:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-42">**Realtime APIs**</a>: Call realtime APIs launched by OpenAI through the integrate websockets server.
README.md:201:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-88">**Guardrails**</a>: Verify your LLM inputs and outputs to adhere to your specified checks. Choose from the 40+ pre-built guardrails to ensure compliance with security and accuracy standards. You can <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-43">bring your own guardrails</a> or choose from our <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-44">many partners</a>.
README.md:202:- [**Secure Key Management**](https://portkey.wiki/gh-45): Use your own keys or generate virtual keys on the fly.
README.md:203:- [**Role-based access control**](https://portkey.wiki/gh-46): Granular access control for your users, workspaces and API keys.
README.md:204:- <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-47">**Compliance & Data Privacy**</a>: The AI gateway is SOC2, HIPAA, GDPR, and CCPA compliant.
README.md:207:- [**Smart caching**](https://portkey.wiki/gh-48): Cache responses from LLMs to reduce costs and improve latency. Supports simple and semantic* caching.
README.md:208:- [**Usage analytics**](https://portkey.wiki/gh-49): Monitor and analyze your AI and LLM usage, including request volume, latency, costs and error rates.
README.md:209:- [**Provider optimization***](https://portkey.wiki/gh-89): Automatically switch to the most cost-effective provider based on usage patterns and pricing models.
README.md:212:- <a href="https://portkey.ai/docs/integrations/agents">**Agents Support**</a>: Seamlessly integrate with popular agent frameworks to build complex AI applications. The gateway seamlessly integrates with [Autogen](https://portkey.wiki/gh-50), [CrewAI](https://portkey.wiki/gh-51), [LangChain](https://portkey.wiki/gh-52), [LlamaIndex](https://portkey.wiki/gh-53), [Phidata](https://portkey.wiki/gh-54), [Control Flow](https://portkey.wiki/gh-55), and even [Custom Agents](https://portkey.wiki/gh-56).
README.md:213:- [**Prompt Template Management***](https://portkey.wiki/gh-57): Create, manage and version your prompt templates collaboratively through a universal prompt playground.

docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:2:title: "Retries & Fallbacks"
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:3:description: "Automatic retry with exponential backoff and provider failover. Retries handle transient errors within a provider; fallbacks switch to a different provider when all retries are exhausted."
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:11:- **Retries** - When a provider returns a transient error (network issue, rate limit, 5xx), Bifrost automatically retries the same request against the same provider with exponential backoff. On rate-limit errors, it can also rotate to a different API key from your pool.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:12:- **Fallbacks** - When the primary provider fails after exhausting all retries, Bifrost moves on to the next provider in your fallback chain. Each fallback provider gets its own full retry budget.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:14:Together, they let you build LLM-powered applications that stay up through rate limits, transient outages, and even full provider failures - with no changes required in your application code.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:25:2. Retries the request against the same provider
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:26:3. On **rate-limit errors** (`429`): rotates to a different API key from the pool (if multiple keys are configured) so fresh capacity is used
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:27:4. On **network/server errors** (`5xx`, DNS, connection refused): reuses the same key - these are transient server issues, not per-key capacity problems
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:48:| Condition | Retried? | Key rotation? |
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:50:| Network error (DNS, connection refused) | Yes | No - same key reused |
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:51:| `5xx` server errors (500, 502, 503, 504) | Yes | No - same key reused |
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:52:| Rate limit (`429` or rate-limit message pattern) | Yes | Yes - next key from pool |
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:59:Retries are configured per-provider in `network_config`. The defaults are `max_retries: 0` (no retries), `retry_backoff_initial: 500` ms, and `retry_backoff_max: 5000` ms.

docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:183:## Fallbacks
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:185:Fallbacks provide automatic failover to a different provider when the primary fails after exhausting all its retries. Each fallback is tried in order until one succeeds.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:187:### How fallbacks work
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:189:1. **Primary attempt**: Tries your configured provider with its full retry budget
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:190:2. **Fallback decision**: If the primary fails (and the error is retryable at the provider level), Bifrost moves to the first fallback
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:191:3. **Sequential fallbacks**: Each fallback provider also gets its own full retry budget
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:192:4. **First success wins**: Returns the response from the first provider that succeeds
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:193:5. **All fail**: Returns the original error from the primary provider. Exception: if a plugin on a fallback provider sets `AllowFallbacks = false` on the error (e.g. a security or compliance plugin that should halt the chain regardless of remaining fallbacks), Bifrost stops immediately and returns that fallback's error rather than continuing to the next provider or returning the primary error.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:195:Each fallback is treated as a completely fresh request - all configured plugins (semantic caching, governance, logging) run again for the fallback provider.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:199:<Tabs group="fallbacks">

docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:309:## How retries and fallbacks work together
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:311:The two mechanisms form a nested resilience loop. Retries run inside each provider attempt; fallbacks run across providers once retries are exhausted.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:317:    participant Primary as Primary Provider
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:318:    participant FB1 as Fallback 1
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:319:    participant FB2 as Fallback 2
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:321:    App->>Bifrost: Request (primary + fallbacks)
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:324:        note over Bifrost,Primary: Primary provider attempt (with retries)
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:326:        Primary-->>Bifrost: 429 Rate Limit
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:327:        note over Bifrost: Backoff + rotate key
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:328:        Bifrost->>Primary: Attempt 2 (different key)
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:337:        note over Bifrost,FB1: Fallback 1 attempt (with its own retries)
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:345:    Bifrost-->>App: Response (from Fallback 1)
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:348:**Key point:** each provider in the chain - primary and every fallback - gets its own full `max_retries` budget. A primary configured with `max_retries: 3` and two fallbacks each also configured with `max_retries: 3` means up to 12 total attempts before giving up.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:351:The retry budget is set per-provider in `network_config`. If your fallback providers have different retry configurations, each will use their own settings.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:358:**Scenario 1: Rate limiting with key rotation**
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:360:OpenAI key 1 hits its rate limit. Bifrost rotates to key 2 on the next retry - no fallback needed, the request succeeds within the same provider.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:362:**Scenario 2: Provider outage**
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:364:OpenAI is experiencing downtime (returning `503`). Bifrost retries with the same key (transient server issue), exhausts `max_retries`, then fails over to Anthropic. Anthropic succeeds on the first attempt.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:368:Both primary and first fallback are down. Bifrost works through each provider's retry budget sequentially until the second fallback succeeds.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:370:**Scenario 4: Cost-sensitive fallback**
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:372:Primary: a premium model for quality. Fallback: a cost-effective alternative. Governance rules can trigger a budget-exceeded error on the primary, which cascades into the fallback chain.
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:378:When a fallback is triggered, the fallback request is treated as completely new:
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:380:- Semantic cache checks run again (the fallback provider may have a cached response)
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:381:- Governance rules apply to the new provider
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:382:- Logging captures the fallback attempt separately
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:383:- All configured plugins execute fresh for each provider in the chain
docs\features\retries-and-fallbacks.mdx:385:**Plugin fallback control:** Plugins can prevent fallbacks from being triggered for specific error types. For example, a security plugin might disable fallbacks for compliance reasons. When a plugin sets `AllowFallbacks = false` on the error, the fallback chain is skipped entirely and the original error is returned immediately.

docs\mcp\gateway-url.mdx:308:The `WWW-Authenticate` URL above and the `redirect_uri` Bifrost hands to upstream OAuth providers (Notion, Jira, etc.) are both built from the request's `Host` header by default. docs\mcp\gateway-url.mdx:311:- `mcp_external_client_url` - what Bifrost registers as the `redirect_uri` with upstream OAuth providers.
docs\mcp\gateway-url.mdx:316:**Changing `mcp_external_client_url` breaks already-connected MCP clients.** Upstream OAuth providers lock the `redirect_uri` to whatever was registered during Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591). If you change this URL afterwards, existing clients fail with **"Invalid redirect URI"** at the authorize step. To recover, clear the stored OAuth client credentials for the affected MCP server and re-authorize so Bifrost re-registers with the new URL.

docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:484:### Making Virtual Keys Mandatory
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:486:All governance-enabled requests must include the virtual key header:
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:498:By default governance is optional, meaning that if the virtual key header is not present, the request will be allowed but without any governance checks/routing. But you can make it mandatory by enforcing the virtual key header.
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:505:2. Check the **Enforce Virtual Keys** checkbox
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:507:![Enforce Virtual Keys](../../media/ui-enforce-virtual-keys.png)
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:537:### Authentication and Virtual Keys
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:539:Virtual keys and HTTP authentication are **independent layers** that can work together:
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:544:| **Virtual Keys** | Request routing and governance | `x-bf-vk`, `Authorization`[^1], `x-api-key`, `x-goog-api-key` |
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:546:[^1]: Authorization can carry virtual keys only when auth is disabled (`disable_auth_on_inference: true`). When auth is enabled, Authorization is consumed by authentication and cannot be used for virtual keys.
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:550:Virtual keys can be passed via any supported header without additional authentication:
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:555:  -H "x-bf-vk: <VIRTUAL_KEY>" \
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:561:  -H "Authorization: Bearer <VIRTUAL_KEY>" \
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:566:### Listing models with a virtual key
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:568:When you call `GET /v1/models` with a virtual key, Bifrost **only lists (and only queries) providers that are allowed by that virtual key**. This avoids unnecessary “provider not allowed” errors in logs and keeps error-rate metrics meaningful.
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:571:# Lists models across providers allowed by the virtual key
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:573:  -H "x-bf-vk: <VIRTUAL_KEY>"
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:576:If you specify a provider explicitly via `?provider=...`, that provider must still be allowed by the virtual key or the request will be rejected:
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:579:# If "anthropic" is not configured/allowed on this virtual key, this returns 403
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:580:curl -sS "http://localhost:8080/v1/models?provider=anthropic" \
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:581:  -H "x-bf-vk: <VIRTUAL_KEY>"
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:586:You must provide both authentication credentials AND the virtual key. Use `x-bf-vk` for the virtual key since the `Authorization` header is used for authentication:
docs\features\governance\virtual-keys.mdx:591:  -H "x-bf-vk: <VIRTUAL_KEY>" \

docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:3:description: "Direct requests to specific AI models, providers, and keys using Virtual Keys."
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:8:**Looking for comprehensive provider routing documentation?**
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:10:For a detailed guide covering governance-based routing, adaptive load balancing, Model Catalog, and how they interact, see the [**Provider Routing Guide**](/providers/provider-routing).
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:12:This page focuses specifically on configuring governance routing via Virtual Keys.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:17:Bifrost's governance-based routing capabilities offer granular control over how requests are directed to different AI models and providers through Virtual Key configuration. By configuring routing rules on a Virtual Key, you can enforce which providers and models are accessible, implement weighted load balancing strategies, create automatic fallbacks, and restrict access to specific provider API keys.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:19:This powerful feature enables key use cases like:
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:21:- **Resilience & Failover**: Automatically fall back to a secondary provider if the primary one fails.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:22:- **Environment Separation**: Dedicate specific virtual keys to development, testing, and production environments with different provider and key access.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:23:- **Cost Management**: Route traffic to cheaper models or providers based on weights to optimize costs.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:24:- **Fine-grained Access Control**: Ensure that different teams or applications only use the models and API keys they are explicitly permitted to.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:26:## Provider/Model Restrictions
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:28:Virtual Keys can be restricted to use only specific provider/models. When provider/model restrictions are configured, the VK can only access those designated provider/models, providing fine-grained control over which provider/models different users or applications can utilize.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:31:- **No Provider Configs** (default): VK **blocks all providers** (deny-by-default). You must add provider configurations to allow traffic.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:32:- **With Provider Configs**: VK limited to only the specified provider/models. Configured providers participate in weighted load balancing only if their `weight` is set to a numeric value, while providers with `weight: null` remain configured but are opted out of weighted selection.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:35:When you configure provider restrictions on a Virtual Key, Bifrost validates that the requested model is allowed for the selected provider:
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:36:- **`allowed_models: ["*"]`**: Allow all models supported by the provider (uses the Model Catalog for validation).
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:39:- **Model Catalog Sync**: On startup and provider updates, Bifrost calls each provider's list models API. If this fails, you'll see a warning: `{"level":"warn","message":"failed to list models for provider <name>: failed to execute HTTP request to provider API"}`
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:42:**Cross-provider routing does NOT happen automatically**. For example, requests for `gpt-4o` will NOT be routed to Anthropic unless you explicitly add `"gpt-4o"` to Anthropic's `allowed_models` in the Virtual Key configuration. Each provider only handles models it actually supports (determined by the Model Catalog).
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:45:## Weighted Load Balancing
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:47:When you configure multiple providers on a Virtual Key, Bifrost automatically implements weighted load balancing. Each provider can be assigned a weight, and requests are distributed proportionally. The `weight` field is optional - omitting it (or setting it to `null`) excludes the provider from weighted selection while still allowing it to be used for direct `provider/model` requests or as a fallback.

docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:212:## API Key Restrictions
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:214:Virtual Keys can be restricted to use only specific provider API keys. When key restrictions are configured, the VK can only access those designated keys, providing fine-grained control over which API keys different users or applications can utilize.
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:217:- **No Restrictions** (`key_ids: ["*"]`): VK can use any available provider keys based on load balancing
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:218:- **With Restrictions**: VK limited to only the specified key IDs, regardless of other available keys
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:219:- **All Blocked** (`key_ids: []` or field omitted): VK cannot use any provider keys (deny-by-default)
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:223:Available Provider Keys:
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:224:├── key-prod-001 → sk-prod-key... (Production OpenAI key)
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:225:├── key-dev-002  → sk-dev-key...  (Development OpenAI key)  
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:226:└── key-test-003 → sk-test-key... (Testing OpenAI key)
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:228:Virtual Key Restrictions:
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:231:│   └── Restricted Keys: [key-prod-001] ← ONLY production key
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:234:│   └── Restricted Keys: [key-dev-002, key-test-003] ← Dev + test keys
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:237:    └── Restricted Keys: ["*"] ← Can use ANY available key
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:242:# Production VK - will ONLY use key-prod-001
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:247:# Development VK - will load balance between key-dev-002 and key-test-003
docs\features\governance\routing.mdx:252:# VK with key_ids: ["*"] - can use any available OpenAI key

docs\features\keys-management.mdx:3:description: "Intelligent API key management with weighted load balancing, model-specific filtering, and automatic failover. Distribute traffic across multiple keys for optimal performance and reliability."
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:7:## Weighted Load Balancing
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:9:Bifrost uses weighted random selection to distribute requests across multiple keys. This allows you to:
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:12:- Assign higher weights to premium keys with better rate limits
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:13:- Balance between production and backup keys
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:14:- Gradually migrate traffic during key rotation
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:18:Key 1: Weight 0.7 (70% probability)
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:19:Key 2: Weight 0.3 (30% probability)
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:26:1. Calculate total weight of all eligible keys
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:28:3. Select key based on cumulative weight ranges
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:29:4. If selected key fails, automatic fallback to next available key
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:33:Keys can be restricted to specific models for access control and cost management:
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:37:- **Populated `models` array**: Key only supports listed models
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:38:- **`blacklisted_models`**: Optional per-key denylist. If non-empty and the requested model appears in it, the key is excluded-even if that model is also in `models` (denylist wins over the allowlist)
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:39:- **Model mismatch**: Key is excluded from selection for that request
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:42:- **Premium Models**: Dedicated keys for expensive models (GPT-4, Claude-3)
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:43:- **Team Separation**: Different keys for different teams or projects
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:45:- **Compliance**: Separate keys for different security requirements
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:46:- **Denylist**: Block specific models on a key
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:50:Each key is created individually via `POST /api/providers/{provider}/keys`:
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:53:// Premium-only key
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:55:  "name": "openai-pre-key-1",
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:56:  "value": "premium-key",
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:61:// Standard-only key
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:63:  "name": "openai-std-key-1",
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:64:  "value": "standard-key",
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:69:// Shared key with denylist
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:71:  "name": "openai-shared-key",
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:72:  "value": "env.OPENAI_API_KEY",
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:81:For cloud providers with deployment-based routing, Bifrost validates deployment availability:
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:84:- Keys must have deployment mappings for specific models
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:86:- Missing deployment excludes key from selection
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:94:1. Check if provider uses deployments (Azure/Bedrock)
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:96:3. Exclude keys without proper deployment mapping
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:99:## Custom Key Usage (By Name or ID)
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:101:Bifrost supports referencing a stored provider key by name or by ID instead of sending the raw secret. This can be useful when you want callers to reference logical key names or stable IDs and let the gateway resolve the actual secret from configured provider keys.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:107:- Header: send `x-bf-api-key-id: <key-id>` on the request. The gateway will look up the key with that ID.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:112:ctx = context.WithValue(ctx, schemas.BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyID, "key-uuid-1234")
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:117:- Header: send `x-bf-api-key: <key-name>` on the request. The gateway will look up the named key and use its secret for the upstream provider call.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:122:ctx = context.WithValue(ctx, schemas.BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyName, "openai-key-1")
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:125:Note: Both mechanisms reference a stored key (not the raw secret). The gateway resolves the key against configured provider keys and applies model allowlists, denylists, and deployment mapping. When an explicit key ID or name is supplied, weighted selection is bypassed and the referenced key is used directly.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:128:# Example: request referencing a stored key name that doesn't exist

docs\features\keys-management.mdx:144:# Example: request referencing a stored key name that exists but no configured keys support the requested model

docs\features\keys-management.mdx:164:## Direct Key Bypass — Removed in v1.5
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:167:The "Direct Key Bypass" feature has been **removed entirely in v1.5**, on both the HTTP gateway and the Go SDK.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:169:- **HTTP gateway:** the `allow_direct_keys` config flag and the `Authorization` / `x-api-key` / `x-goog-api-key` header pass-through (plus the Bedrock `x-bf-bedrock-*` and Azure `x-bf-azure-endpoint` integration paths) no longer forward keys to upstream providers.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:170:- **Go SDK:** the `schemas.BifrostContextKeyDirectKey` context value and the `Direct Key (Go SDK Only)` API have been removed.
docs\features\keys-management.mdx:172:All requests must use Bifrost-managed provider keys. To pin a specific key per request from the Go SDK, set `schemas.BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyID` or `schemas.BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyName` against a key managed by Bifrost (for example, one created via the providers API or returned by your `Account` implementation). See the [v1.5.0 migration guide](/migration-guides/v1.5.0) for the full rationale and migration recipes.
docs\deployment-guides\config-json\client.mdx:15:| `initial_pool_size` | integer | `300` | Pre-allocated worker goroutines per provider queue |
docs\deployment-guides\config-json\client.mdx:16:| `drop_excess_requests` | boolean | `false` | Drop requests when queue is full instead of waiting (returns HTTP 429) |
docs\deployment-guides\config-json\client.mdx:18:A larger pool reduces latency spikes under burst load at the cost of higher baseline memory. `500–1000` is a common starting point for production workloads with multiple providers.

It is the `redirect_uri` Bifrost registers with Notion, Jira, GitHub, etc. when it acts as an OAuth client to an MCP server. Upstream providers redirect the user's browser to `<client URL>/api/oauth/callback` after login.

docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:49:## Budget Management
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:54:- **Provider Pricing** - Real-time model pricing data
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:62:### Budget Checking Flow
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:64:When a request is made with a virtual key, Bifrost checks **all applicable budgets independently** in the hierarchy. Each budget must have sufficient remaining balance for the request to proceed.
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:70:1. ✓ Provider Config Budget (if provider config has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:71:2. ✓ VK Budget (if VK has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:72:3. ✓ Team Budget (if VK's team has budget)  
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:73:4. ✓ Customer Budget (if team's customer has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:78:1. ✓ Provider Config Budget (if provider config has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:79:2. ✓ VK Budget (if VK has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:80:3. ✓ Customer Budget (if VK's customer has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:85:1. ✓ Provider Config Budget (if provider config has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:86:2. ✓ VK Budget (if VK has budget)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:90:- **All applicable budgets must pass** - any single budget failure blocks the request
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:91:- **Budgets are independent** - each tracks its own usage and limits
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:92:- **Costs are deducted from all applicable budgets** - same cost applied to each level
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:93:- **Rate limits checked at provider config and VK levels** - teams and customers have no rate limits
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:94:- **Provider selection** - providers that exceed their budget or rate limits are excluded from [routing](./routing)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:98:- Provider config budget: $4/$5 remaining ✓
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:99:- VK budget: $9/$10 remaining ✓
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:100:- Team budget: $15/$20 remaining ✓  
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:101:- Customer budget: $45/$50 remaining ✓
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:102:- Result: Allowed (no budget is exceeded)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:106:    - Updated Provider=$6/$5, VK=$11/$10, Team=$17/$20, Customer=$47/$50
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:107:    - Then the next request will be blocked (both provider and VK budgets exceeded).
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:110:## Rate Limiting
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:112:Rate limits protect your system from abuse and manage traffic by setting thresholds on request frequency and token usage over a specific time window. Rate limits can be configured at **both the Virtual Key level and Provider Config level** for granular control.
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:114:Bifrost supports two types of rate limits that work in parallel:
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:118:### Rate Limit Hierarchy
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:120:Rate limits are checked in hierarchical order:
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:122:1. ✓ Provider Config Rate Limits (if provider config has rate limits)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:123:2. ✓ Virtual Key Rate Limits (if VK has rate limits)
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:126:For a request to be allowed, it must pass both the request limit and token limit checks at **all applicable levels**. If a provider config exceeds its rate limits, that provider is excluded from routing, but other providers within the same virtual key remain available.
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:128:### Provider-Level Rate Limiting
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:130:Provider configs within a virtual key can have independent rate limits, enabling:
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:131:- **Per-Provider Throttling**: Different rate limits for OpenAI vs Anthropic
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:132:- **Provider Isolation**: Rate limit violations on one provider don't affect others
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:133:- **Granular Control**: Fine-tune limits based on provider capabilities and costs
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:137:Budgets and rate limits support flexible reset durations:
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:149:- **Rate Limits**: `1m`, `1h`, `1d` for request throttling
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:150:- **Budgets**: `1d`, `1w`, `1M`, `1Y` for cost control
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:152:### Calendar-aligned budgets
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:154:By default, a budget **rolls**: after `reset_duration` elapses since `last_reset`, usage resets. With **`calendar_aligned`: `true`**, the budget resets at the **start of each calendar period in UTC** instead (same instant for every customer of that configuration).
docs\features\governance\budget-and-limits.mdx:158:Calendar alignment applies to budgets on **customers**, **teams**, **virtual keys**, and **per–provider-config** budgets. You can set it when creating a budget (`calendar_aligned` on create) or toggle it on update (`calendar_aligned` on the budget in `PUT` requests). Turning calendar alignment **on** for an existing budget resets **current usage to zero** and snaps **`last_reset`** to the current period start.

docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:9:**Bifrost Clustering** delivers production-ready high availability through a peer-to-peer network architecture with automatic service discovery. The clustering system uses gossip protocols to maintain consistent state across nodes while providing seamless scaling, automatic failover, and zero-downtime deployments.
docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:17:| **Single Point of Failure** | Complete service outage if gateway fails | Distributed architecture with automatic failover |
docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:19:| **Provider Rate Limits** | Request throttling and service interruption | Distributed rate limit tracking across cluster |

docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:44:- Handles failover automatically
docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:53:| **gRPC counter sync** | `10102` (TCP) | Application messages: governance usage counters, config sync, routing rules, virtual keys, providers, RBAC, MCP tools, pricing, auth config, and 25+ other replicated entity types |
docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:59:Each replicated message carries an `EntityType` identifying the kind of state being broadcast. Bifrost replicates 30+ entity types across the cluster, including: model catalog, virtual keys, providers, governance counters, routing rules, RBAC, MCP tools and tool groups, pricing and pricing overrides, access profiles, prompt deployments, auth configuration, and cluster diagnostics. See the [Replicated Entity Types](#replicated-entity-types) reference for the complete list.
docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:63:Each broadcast carries a unique message ID and a `SentAt` timestamp. Receivers run a deduper (default 5-minute TTL) keyed by message ID, so a node that has already processed a given message ignores re-broadcasts of the same ID. When a newer message with the same ID arrives, the existing entry is invalidated and replaced.
docs\enterprise\clustering.mdx:83:Election is deterministic: the lexicographically-first healthy member wins. The election loop re-evaluates membership every 30 seconds, so leadership transfers automatically when nodes join, leave, or fail. There is nothing to configure - leader election runs whenever clustering is enabled.

docs\features\async-inference.mdx:164:## Virtual Key Authorization
docs\features\async-inference.mdx:166:- If a job is created with a virtual key, the job stores that virtual key identity.
docs\features\async-inference.mdx:167:- Polling must use the same virtual key value.
docs\features\async-inference.mdx:168:- Missing or mismatched virtual keys fail lookup and return `404 Job not found or expired`.
docs\features\async-inference.mdx:169:- Jobs created without a virtual key are not virtual-key scoped, so they can be polled by any caller that passes your gateway auth/middleware checks.

docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:3:description: "Advanced load balancing algorithms with predictive scaling, health monitoring, and performance optimization for enterprise-grade traffic distribution."

docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:12:This page focuses on the technical implementation and performance characteristics of adaptive load balancing.
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:17:**Adaptive Load Balancing** in Bifrost Enterprise automatically optimizes traffic distribution across providers and keys based on real-time performance metrics. The system operates at **two levels** - provider selection (direction) and key selection (route) - continuously monitoring error rates, latency, and throughput to dynamically adjust weights, ensuring optimal performance and reliability.
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:19:### Key Features
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:23:| **Dynamic Weight Adjustment** | Automatically adjusts key weights based on performance metrics |
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:24:| **Real-time Performance Monitoring** | Tracks error rates, latency, and success rates per model-key combination |
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:26:| **Circuit Breaker Integration** | Temporarily removes poorly performing keys from rotation |
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:37:The load balancing system operates at two levels:
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:39:- **Direction-level** (provider + model): Decides which provider to use for a given model
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:40:- **Route-level** (provider + model + key): Decides which API key to use within a provider
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:42:This two-tier approach enables both macro-level provider selection and micro-level key optimization.
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:49:        DS["Provider Selector<br/>Score-based selection"]
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:56:        RS["Key Selector<br/>Weighted random"]
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:57:        K1["Key 1<br/>weight: 850"]
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:58:        K2["Key 2<br/>weight: 620"]
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:59:        K3["Key 3<br/>weight: 45"]
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:134:## Key Capabilities
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:136:1. **Automatic Route Health Management**: Routes automatically transition between 4 states (Healthy, Degraded, Failed, Recovering) based on error rates and latency. No manual intervention required when a route fails or recovers.
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:143:  <img src="/media/ui-load-balancing.png" alt="Adaptive Load Balancing Dashboard" />
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:148:5. **Smart Key Selection**: Uses weighted random selection with jitter (5% band) and 25% exploration probability to probe potentially recovered routes, rather than always picking the best route.
docs\enterprise\adaptive-load-balancing.mdx:150:6. **Performance Thresholds**: Specific triggers drive state transitions -&gt; 2% error rate triggers Degraded, &gt;5% error rate or TPM hit triggers Failed, &lt;2% error with 50%+ expected traffic triggers Healthy.

docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:664:Send custom headers with individual requests using the `x-bf-eh-*` prefix. Headers are automatically propagated to the provider after stripping the prefix. This is useful for request-specific metadata, user identification, or custom tracking information.
docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:679:The `x-bf-eh-` prefix is stripped before forwarding, so `x-bf-eh-user-id` becomes `user-id` in the request to the provider.
docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:690:Bifrost maintains a security denylist of headers that are never forwarded to providers, regardless of configuration:
docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:701:    // prevent auth/key overrides via x-bf-eh-*
docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:702:    "x-api-key":      true,
docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:703:    "x-goog-api-key": true,
docs\quickstart\gateway\provider-configuration.mdx:704:    "x-bf-api-key":   true,

docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:43:#### Non-OpenAI-compatible Providers
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:45:If the provider has a **custom API format** (not OpenAI-compatible), create a new folder `core/providers/[provider_name]/`.
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:47:**Complete Reference Structure** (see `core/providers/huggingface/`):
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:50:core/providers/

docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:53:    ├── [provider_name]_test.go     # Provider automated tests (REQUIRED)
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:54:    ├── types.go                    # ALL provider-specific types/structs (REQUIRED)
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:69:1. Create `types.go` FIRST - Define all provider-specific request/response structures
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:72:4. Create `[provider_name].go` FOURTH - Wire everything together
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:73:5. Create `[provider_name]_test.go` LAST - Add comprehensive tests
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:75:#### OpenAI-compatible Providers
docs\contributing\adding-a-provider.mdx:77:If the provider is **OpenAI API compatible**, you only need a minimal structure:

docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:89:## Breaking Change 2: `allowed_keys` Renamed to `key_ids`
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:91:The field used to restrict which provider API keys a Virtual Key can use has been renamed from `allowed_keys` to `key_ids`. The deny-by-default rule also applies - omitting the field or setting it to `[]` now blocks all keys.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:94:Unlike `allowed_models`, there is no automatic database migration for `key_ids`. An empty or omitted `key_ids` disables all key selection. You must explicitly use `["*"]` to restore allow-all behavior.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:99:{ "provider": "openai", "allowed_keys": ["key-prod-001"], "weight": 1.0 }
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:104:{ "provider": "openai", "key_ids": ["key-prod-001"], "allowed_models": ["*"], "weight": 1.0 }
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:107:To allow all keys:
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:109:{ "provider": "openai", "key_ids": ["*"], "allowed_models": ["*"], "weight": 1.0 }
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:114:## Breaking Change 3: Virtual Key `provider_configs` is Deny-by-Default
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:116:In v1.4.x, a Virtual Key with no `provider_configs` had access to all providers. In v1.5.0, it blocks all providers.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:118:**Before:** `"provider_configs": []` → access to all providers
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:120:**After:** `"provider_configs": []` → no provider access
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:122:To allow all providers, list each one explicitly:
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:125:  "provider_configs": [
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:126:    { "provider": "openai",    "allowed_models": ["*"], "key_ids": ["*"], "weight": 1.0 },
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:127:    { "provider": "anthropic", "allowed_models": ["*"], "key_ids": ["*"], "weight": 1.0 }
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:132:The automatic migration backfills all currently configured providers into any VK that has an empty `provider_configs`. However, any VK created after upgrading must include explicit provider configs.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:155:Applies to: `models`, `allowed_models`, `key_ids`, `tools_to_execute`, `tools_to_auto_execute`, `allowed_extra_headers`.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:161:The `weight` field on a Virtual Key provider config was previously a required `float64`. It is now an optional `*float64`.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:163:- `weight: 0.5` - provider participates in weighted load balancing
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:164:- `weight: null` / omitted - provider is accessible for direct routing but excluded from weighted selection
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:170:## Breaking Change 6: Virtual Key `budget` Changed to Multi-Budget `budgets`
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:172:The budget model on Virtual Keys and provider configs has been restructured from a single budget to support multiple budgets with different reset intervals.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:174:In v1.4.x, a Virtual Key had a single `budget_id` foreign key pointing to one budget, and each provider config also had a single `budget_id`. In v1.5.0, the association is inverted: budgets now reference their parent via `virtual_key_id` or `provider_config_id`, and both Virtual Keys and provider configs support an array of budgets.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:176:The database migration runs automatically on startup, converting existing single-budget associations into the new multi-budget structure.

docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:548:## Breaking Change 13: `selected_key_id` Cleared on Terminal Retry Failures
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:550:With the introduction of multi-key retry rotation, `selected_key_id` (and `selected_key_name`) in the request context are **cleared when all retry attempts fail**. Previously, these fields always reflected the key that was selected for the request, even on error.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:552:The `attempt_trail` is now the authoritative record of every key tried and why each attempt failed.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:558:| `selected_key_id` | Always set, even on error | Empty string when all retries exhausted |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:559:| `selected_key_name` | Always set, even on error | Empty string when all retries exhausted |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:560:| `attempt_trail` | Not present | Array of `{ key_id, key_name, fail_reason }` per attempt |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:564:The built-in **logging plugin** writes `selected_key_id` and `selected_key_name` directly to each log record. For multi-key requests that exhaust all retries, both fields will be empty in the stored log entry. The `attempt_trail` column captures the full per-attempt key history and is the correct field to use for failure attribution.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:566:The built-in **telemetry plugin** emits `selected_key_id` and `selected_key_name` as span attributes. For exhausted-retry failures these attributes will be empty strings on the error span. The `attempt_trail` span attribute contains the full rotation history.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:568:If you run a custom plugin or downstream log consumer that filters or groups by `selected_key_id` to track which key caused a failure, you must update it to handle the empty-string case and read from `attempt_trail` when attribution is needed.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:572:**If you read `selected_key_id` from plugin context to attribute failed requests:**
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:576:keyID, _ := ctx.Value(schemas.BifrostContextKeySelectedKeyID).(string)
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:577:// keyID was always populated, even on error
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:582:// Populated on success (or for single-key / pinned / sticky flows on error):
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:583:keyID, _ := ctx.Value(schemas.BifrostContextKeySelectedKeyID).(string)
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:586:if trail, ok := ctx.Value(schemas.BifrostContextKeyAttemptTrail).([]schemas.KeyAttemptRecord); ok {
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:588:        // record.KeyID, record.KeyName, record.FailReason
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:593:**If you consume `selected_key_id` from the logging REST API:**
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:595:The `selected_key_id` field on a `LogEntry` may now be an empty string when the request failed after exhausting all retries. Use `attempt_trail` for the full per-attempt key history.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:598:Single-key, pinned (`x-bf-key-id` / `x-bf-key-name`), and session-sticky requests are unaffected - they never rotate keys, so `selected_key_id` remains populated on failure for those flows.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:603:## Breaking Change 14: Direct Key Bypass Removed (HTTP Gateway and Go SDK)
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:605:The "Direct Key Bypass" feature has been **removed entirely** in v1.5.0, on both surfaces:
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:607:- **HTTP gateway:** the `allow_direct_keys` config flag and the header pass-through (`Authorization`, `x-api-key`, `x-goog-api-key`, plus the Bedrock `x-bf-bedrock-*` and Azure `x-bf-azure-endpoint` integration paths) no longer forward keys to upstream providers.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:608:- **Go SDK:** the `schemas.BifrostContextKeyDirectKey` context value has been deleted, along with the documented "Direct Key (Go SDK Only)" API.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:610:**All requests must now resolve to a Bifrost-managed provider key**, either implicitly (the configured key pool plus weighted selection) or by pinning a registered key via `BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyID` / `BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyName` (Go SDK) or virtual keys (`sk-bf-*`, HTTP).
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:616:| `client.allow_direct_keys` in `config.json` | **Removed** — field is no longer recognized; ignored if present |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:617:| `client_config.allow_direct_keys` over `PUT /api/config` | **Removed** — field is dropped from the request payload |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:618:| Web UI **Settings → Security → "Allow Direct API Keys"** toggle | **Removed** |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:619:| `Authorization: Bearer sk-...` header → upstream provider | **No longer forwarded** as a direct key. Bearer values starting with `sk-bf-` continue to work as virtual keys |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:620:| `x-api-key` / `x-goog-api-key` header → upstream provider | **No longer forwarded** as a direct key |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:621:| `x-bf-bedrock-api-key` / `x-bf-bedrock-access-key` / `x-bf-bedrock-secret-key` / `x-bf-bedrock-session-token` / `x-bf-bedrock-region` | **No longer extracted** by the Bedrock integration |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:622:| `x-bf-azure-endpoint` + bare Authorization header on Azure OpenAI integration routes | **No longer extracted** as a direct Azure key |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:623:| Database column `config_client.allow_direct_keys` | **Auto-dropped** on first startup of v1.5.0 |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:624:| `schemas.BifrostContextKeyDirectKey` (Go SDK constant) | **Removed** — code referencing it will fail to compile |
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:625:| `Bifrost.getAllSupportedKeys` / `getKeysForBatchAndFileOps` / `selectKeyFromProviderForModelWithPool` DirectKey branches | **Removed** — these no longer special-case a caller-supplied key |

docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:678:**For providers that allow keyless requests** (ambient credentials, IAM roles, etc.), `BifrostContextKeySkipKeySelection` is unchanged.
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:682:The direct-key path bypassed Bifrost's key management entirely, which meant:
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:684:- **No governance** — virtual key budgets, rate limits, provider/model allow-lists, and routing rules were not applied to direct-key traffic
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:685:- **No rotation or fallback** — direct keys were used as-is with no retry across alternate keys
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:686:- **No observability attribution** — header-provided keys had a synthetic `key_id: "header-provided"` that defeated per-key cost and usage analytics
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:687:- **Security surface area** — a misconfigured HTTP deployment could leak provider credentials through logs or proxy chains; the Go SDK equivalent had the same hazard for any caller logging context contents
docs\migration-guides\v1.5.0.mdx:689:The supported `BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyID` / `BifrostContextKeyAPIKeyName` path covers the "pick a specific key per request" use case without the governance and observability gaps.

docs\providers\test-harness-coverage.mdx:13:**`[PREVIEW]` tag**: requests prefixed `[PREVIEW]` are gated behind `INCLUDE_PREVIEW=1` (default-skipped) because they target account/region-scoped resources — preview-model deployments, vector stores, cached content references, MCP servers — that the harness can't provision in arbitrary environments. Run `make run-provider-harness-test INCLUDE_PREVIEW=1` to include them.

docs\providers\test-harness-coverage.mdx:322:**Bedrock**: passthrough is **not supported by design**. docs\providers\supported-providers\fireworks.mdx:174:For Fireworks chat completions, Bifrost maps `prompt_cache_key` to Fireworks `prompt_cache_isolation_key`, which is the Fireworks body field for cache isolation. Fireworks also accepts the header form `x-prompt-cache-isolation-key`. For text completions, Bifrost extracts `prompt_cache_key` from `extra_params` and maps it to the same Fireworks body field. If you need Fireworks session-affinity behavior, pass `user`, configure `x-session-affinity` in provider extra headers, or send it through the HTTP gateway via `x-bf-eh-x-session-affinity`. Live cache-hit behavior remains model and deployment dependent.

docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:2:title: "Provider Routing"
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:3:description: "Understand how Bifrost routes requests across AI providers using governance rules and adaptive load balancing."
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:9:Bifrost offers two powerful methods for routing requests across AI providers, each serving different use cases:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:11:1. **Governance-based Routing**: Explicit, user-defined routing rules configured via Virtual Keys
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:12:2. **Adaptive Load Balancing**: Automatic, performance-based routing powered by real-time metrics (Enterprise feature)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:14:When both methods are available, **governance takes precedence** because users have explicitly defined their routing preferences through provider configurations on Virtual Keys.
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:19:  - Use **Adaptive Load Balancing** for automatic performance optimization and minimal configuration overhead
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:26:The Model Catalog is Bifrost's central registry that tracks which models are available from which providers. It powers both governance-based routing and adaptive load balancing by maintaining an up-to-date mapping of models to providers.
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:41:   - Contains model names, pricing tiers, and provider mappings
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:43:   - Used for cost calculation and initial model-to-provider mapping
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:44:   - **Stored as**: In-memory map `pricingData[model|provider|mode]` for O(1) lookups
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:46:2. **Provider List Models API** (Secondary source)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:47:   - Calls each provider's `/v1/models` endpoint during startup
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:48:   - Enriches the catalog with provider-specific models and aliases
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:49:   - Re-fetched when providers are added/updated via API or dashboard
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:51:   - **Stored as**: In-memory map `modelPool[provider][]models`
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:61:Bifrost uses a sophisticated multi-step process to determine if a model is available for a provider:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:64:  <Accordion title="GetModelsForProvider(provider)">

docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:832:## Default Provider Resolution
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:835:  Default provider resolution via model catalog is available in **Bifrost
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:839:When a request includes a bare model name without a `provider/` prefix (e.g., `"model": "gpt-4o"` instead of `"model": "openai/gpt-4o"`), Bifrost automatically resolves the provider using the Model Catalog. Note that this default behavior is applied **after all other routing engines** have run.
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:843:1. **Request arrives** without a provider prefix (e.g., `"model": "gpt-4o"`)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:844:2. **Catalog lookup**: Bifrost calls `GetProvidersForModel("gpt-4o")` to find all providers that support the model
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:845:3. **Provider selected**: A provider from the catalog's available list is used (e.g., `openai`)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:846:4. **Request continues**: The resolved `provider/model` string is used for load balancing and fallback handling
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:851:No provider specified for model gpt-4o, found 3 options in model catalog:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:859:# maps gpt-4o → openai as the first provider:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:871:  provider, the request returns an error asking for the `provider/model` format.
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:872:  For deterministic provider selection, always use the explicit `provider/model`
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:880:Governance-based routing allows you to explicitly define which providers and models should handle requests for a specific Virtual Key. This method provides precise control over routing decisions.
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:884:When a Virtual Key has `provider_configs` defined:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:886:1. **Request arrives** with a Virtual Key (e.g., `x-bf-vk: vk-prod-main`)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:887:2. **Model validation**: Bifrost checks if the requested model is allowed for any configured provider
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:888:3. **Provider filtering**: Providers are filtered based on:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:890:   - Budget limits (current usage vs max limit)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:891:   - Rate limits (tokens/requests per time window)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:892:4. **Weighted selection**: A provider is selected using weighted random distribution
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:893:5. **Provider prefix added**: Model string becomes `provider/model` (e.g., `openai/gpt-4o`)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:894:6. **Fallbacks created**: Remaining providers sorted by weight (descending) are added as fallbacks

docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1022:## Adaptive Load Balancing
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1025:  **Enterprise Feature**: Adaptive Load Balancing is available in Bifrost
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1030:Adaptive Load Balancing automatically optimizes routing based on real-time performance metrics. It operates at **two levels** to provide both macro-level provider selection and micro-level key optimization.
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1035:  Separating provider selection (direction) from key selection (route) enables:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1036:  - **Provider-level optimization**: Choose the best provider for a model based on aggregate performance
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1037:  - **Key-level optimization**: Within that provider, choose the best API key based on individual key performance
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1038:  - **Resilience**: Even when provider is specified (by governance or user), key-level load balancing still optimizes which API key to use
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1045:    subgraph Level1["Level 1: Direction (Provider Selection)"]

docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1048:        Filter["Filter by allowed_models<br/>and key availability"]
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1053:    subgraph Level2["Level 2: Route (Key Selection)"]
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1054:        Keys["Available OpenAI Keys:<br/>key-1, key-2, key-3"]
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1055:        KeyScore["Score each key:<br/>error rate, latency, TPM hits"]
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1056:        KeySelect["Select: key-2<br/>(best performing)"]

docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1063:### Level 1: Direction (Provider Selection)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1065:**When it runs**: Only when the model string has **no** provider prefix (e.g., `gpt-4o`)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1069:1. **Model catalog lookup**: Find all configured providers that support the requested model
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1070:2. **Provider filtering**: Filter based on:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1071:   - Allowed models from keys configuration
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1072:   - Keys availability for the provider
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1073:3. **Performance scoring**: Calculate scores for each provider based on:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1078:4. **Smart selection**: Choose provider using weighted random with jitter and exploration
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1079:5. **Fallbacks created**: Remaining providers sorted by performance score (descending) are added as fallbacks
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1081:### Level 2: Route (Key Selection)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1083:**When it runs**: **Always**, even when provider is already specified (by governance, user, or Level 1)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1087:1. **Get available keys**: Fetch all keys for the selected provider
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1088:2. **Filter by configuration**: Apply model restrictions from key configuration
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1089:3. **Performance scoring**: Calculate score for each key based on:
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1092:   - TPM hits (rate limit violations)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1093:   - Current state (Healthy, Degraded, Failed, Recovering)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1094:4. **Weighted random selection**: Choose key with exploration (25% chance to probe recovering keys)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1095:5. **Circuit breaker**: Skip keys with zero weight (TPM hits, repeated failures)
docs\providers\provider-routing.mdx:1099:The load balancer computes a performance score for each provider-model combination:

docs\providers\performance.mdx:9:Bifrost provides three key performance configuration parameters that control throughput, memory usage, and request handling behavior:
docs\providers\performance.mdx:13:| **Concurrency** | Per Provider | 1000 | Number of worker goroutines processing requests simultaneously |
docs\providers\performance.mdx:14:| **Buffer Size** | Per Provider | 5000 | Maximum requests that can be queued before blocking/dropping |
docs\providers\performance.mdx:25:### Concurrency (Per Provider)
docs\providers\performance.mdx:27:**What it does:** Controls two aspects of provider performance:
docs\providers\performance.mdx:28:1. **Worker Goroutines:** The number of goroutines that process requests for each provider. Each worker pulls requests from the provider's queue and executes them against the provider's API.
docs\providers\performance.mdx:29:2. **Provider Pool Pre-warming:** Pre-allocates provider-specific response objects (e.g., `AnthropicMessageResponse`, `OpenAIResponse`) in sync pools to reduce allocations during request handling.
docs\providers\performance.mdx:32:- **Higher concurrency** = More parallel requests to the provider, higher throughput, more pre-allocated response objects
docs\providers\performance.mdx:33:- **Lower concurrency** = Fewer parallel requests, lower resource usage, respects provider rate limits
docs\providers\performance.mdx:35:**Default:** `1000` workers per provider

docs\providers\performance.mdx:72:### Buffer Size (Per Provider)
docs\providers\performance.mdx:74:**What it does:** Sets the capacity of the buffered channel (queue) for each provider. Incoming requests are queued here before being picked up by workers.
docs\providers\performance.mdx:80:**Default:** `5000` requests per provider queue
docs\providers\performance.mdx:87:**Constraint:** Buffer size must be greater than or equal to concurrency. If `concurrency > buffer_size`, provider setup will fail.

docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:144:## Custom Providers
docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:146:In addition to the built-in providers, Bifrost supports custom provider configurations. Custom providers allow you to create multiple instances of the same base provider with different configurations, request type restrictions, and access patterns. This is useful for environment-specific configurations, role-based access control, and feature testing.
docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:148:**Learn more:** [Custom Providers](../custom-providers)

docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:154:- **Provider switching** without code modifications
docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:155:- **Fallback configurations** for improved reliability
docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:156:- **Load balancing** across multiple providers
docs\providers\supported-providers\overview.mdx:157:- **OpenAI-compatible patterns** for all providers
